/content/083d21f8-ac03-4d72-b149-e8ded11.title: Heatwaves spark interest in Gulf-style extreme cooling
articleContent: At sunrise, before Dubai’s megamalls open their doors to the general public, people are already bounding along marbled corridors past the luxury boutiques that forged the city’s reputation as a shoppers’ paradise.

But these are not customers looking for bargains: the emirate’s cavernous shopping centres double as air-conditioned running tracks during the summer, with runners gathering at 6am to escape outside temperatures approaching 40C and compete in races of up to 10km.

Long before Europe’s recent exceptionally hot summers prompted calls for more air conditioning of public and private spaces, Gulf states were investing in homes, offices and infrastructure to help residents cope with the region’s extreme seasonal temperatures.

“There are things that have been done in the Middle East and around the Mediterranean that Europe should pay attention to for its new developments,” said Oscar Brousse, a lecturer in urban climatology and health at University College London.
Runners take part in the “Mallathon” in an air-conditioned Dubai mall to escape the outside heat

There are obvious constraints in both Europe and the Gulf — Brousse said policymakers needed to consider the huge amounts of water and energy needed for cooling projects and the possible unintended consequences for the natural environment.

But Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, which scientists said would have been virtually impossible without climate change, has provoked complaints from tourists and residents about the scarcity of air conditioning.

Dubai has over the past decade invested in chilled walkways that make it easier to go on foot without stepping into the heat outside. The emirate’s “Mallathon” — an indoor run through shopping centres — was launched in 2025.

Abu Dhabi this year opened a 660-metre, air-conditioned, covered walkway in Khalidiyah Park. Nearby King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa Park features a “pocket forest” of drought-tolerant ghaf trees with a smaller open chilled walkway. But a reporter visiting the park in July found it to be almost empty, with the cooling vents in the open air unable to offset the sweltering summer heat.

Qatar also earlier this year unveiled a 450-metre open pathway called Crystal Walk in Doha, where cool air is blown from vents in the ground and artificial metal “trees” are intended to help trap the cool air and offer shade.

However, this kind of evaporative cooling only works well in very dry areas, said Matthaios Santamouris, a professor at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, limiting its potential in parts of Europe.

“Air conditioning outdoor spaces is fundamentally unsustainable,” he said. The amount of energy needed to cool outdoor spaces was too high and not appropriate for large-scale urban projects, he added.
“If our goal is to move towards a zero-carbon society, solutions of this kind should be avoided,” Santamouris said.

For rich Gulf countries using tourism to diversify their economies away from oil and gas, being able to make visitors comfortable at any time of year is increasingly important. Qatar used various cooling technologies when it hosted the 2022 Fifa World Cup in Doha to show that its climate could be compatible with mass tourism. The event was criticised for its environmental cost, even after the tournament was moved to late autumn.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The ultimate goal is to find technologies that use as few resources as possible, while limiting the risks such as the spread of disease from stagnant water left behind by the cooling systems, said Samiullah Khan, chief sustainability officer at UAE infrastructure firm National Development Consortium. There have been real technological advances in these areas, he said.

Khan advised on a project to cool 6,000 cows shipped from Europe to Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates, he said. Before that, he worked on a project to create a chilled platform so that an Emirati royal could comfortably sit and relax in a field of wheat.

One system, developed by US climate-tech company AtmoCooling, releases fine water droplets that evaporate, cooling atmospheric temperatures by as much as 9C — but usually by about 3C to 5C — chief executive and founder Paul Mahacek said. It is being tested in Abu Dhabi’s desert to reduce air temperatures to levels more favourable for crops, he added.

Evaporative cooling technology such as AtmoCooling uses the evaporation of water to cool the air outside rather than air conditioning, which uses refrigeration to cool the air inside buildings.
Santamouris said the latest generation of construction materials, which can be applied to buildings and pavements and reflect solar energy into space, offered the greatest potential.

These coatings, known as supercool materials, have been shown to reduce temperatures when painted on to rooftops in Riyadh, he said. Depending on local climatic conditions, such materials can reduce the surface temperature of cities by up to 15C and could be used in Europe, he added.
European cities have typically turned to nature-based solutions in the past, but once temperatures rise above around 35C, these are no longer enough, said Santamouris.

While outdoor cooling projects are gaining traction in the Middle East, they pale in comparison to indoor projects.

District cooling, which uses pipes of chilled water to cool buildings and benefits from economies of scale like the centralised heating systems used in cold winters in eastern Europe, has expanded significantly in the UAE over the past 15 years.

It is becoming big business for its operators, who are attracted by its long-term concessions and predictable revenue streams. And as Gulf cities continue to expand, demand will increase.

But the applicability of such technologies may be limited in Europe, as the number of days on which indoor cooling is required may be too few to justify the substantial cost of installing the infrastructure.

Nevertheless, outdoor cooling may become more prevalent in the years to come. “We really haven’t done any marketing in Europe,” said AtmoCooling’s Mahacek. “But this summer has been incredible in terms of the interest we’ve received — for agriculture but especially for urban areas.”

/content/5bd905f6-5460-4e76-890f-20746a4.title: Lindsey Graham’s sister wins South Carolina primary
articleContent: Donald Trump clinched a crucial political victory on Tuesday as Darline Graham, the sister of late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, won her Senate primary contest following the president’s full-throated endorsement.

Graham, a political novice who was appointed to replace her brother in South Carolina after his sudden death last month, beat Ralph Norman, a conservative Republican member of Congress who has at times criticised the president and the party’s leadership.
Graham won 52.4 per cent of the vote while Norman recorded 47.6 per cent, according to the Associated Press.
Recommended
Her victory is a sign that Trump retains his hold on right-leaning voters ahead of the November midterm elections as he tries to retain control of Congress during his final two years in office.

Trump was vigorous in his support for Graham in recent weeks, holding a high-profile rally in Myrtle Beach, along the southern state’s coast, and spending more than $800,000 from his main fundraising group, Maga Inc, to prop up her campaign.
Trump celebrated the win on his Truth Social platform, while Graham invoked her late brother in a victory speech in Columbia, South Carolina.
“It’s just not the same without you here,” she told supporters, adding: “I have mixed emotions right now — I’m still feeling grief, heartache and immense gratitude.”

Graham’s candidacy had been dogged by accusations that she was unprepared for the role, concerns that multiplied after she said in a debate that she was “not that informed on national security” in response to a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Her comment not only exposed a critical gap in her knowledge but was also a striking contrast with her late brother, a prominent Republican hawk who played a big role in shaping US foreign and military policy.
Graham attempted to quell the furore surrounding her comments by saying she was not a “career politician”.
Recommended
Trump’s preferred candidates have had mixed results in Republican primary races across the country as the US president struggles with low approval ratings, particularly on the economy.

While the president’s picks successfully unseated intraparty foes in prominent Senate contests in Texas and Louisiana earlier this year, his endorsement failed to help candidates in several governors’ races including in Iowa and Wyoming, as well as several House contests in Florida and Tennessee.

Trump has been under pressure to deploy more of the $400mn war chest assembled by Maga Inc ahead of the midterm elections. The $827,000 expenditure for Graham disclosed by the group was its first big spending move of the midterms campaign.

/content/21080ecd-b261-4b35-994c-20d510f.title: Argentines struggle to repay debts in Milei’s painful economic overhaul
articleContent: When his car broke down in early 2025, Jonatan Verón, a 41-year-old Uber driver in La Plata, Argentina, took out a bank loan of about $1,300 to fix the motor.

Within months, Verón began missing repayments as his income failed to keep pace with living costs. After he burst a tyre, he was forced to borrow an additional $330 from an informal lender at a 300 per cent interest rate. His debts have since ballooned to more than $11,000.
“It’s so much,” said Verón, adding that he also owed money to his sister, ex-wife and mobile phone provider. “But I had no other choice.”
Record numbers of Argentine households are struggling to pay debts on time, with 16.3 per cent of credit issued to individuals at least three months overdue, according to think-tank Equilibra.

The bad loans stem from sweeping changes in Argentina’s economy under libertarian president Javier Milei, who has slashed government spending and lowered annual inflation from a peak of 289 per cent in early 2024 to 34 per cent.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Milei’s economic stabilisation has given banks greater incentive to lend, just as his austerity measures have given many families a greater need to borrow. Argentines had grown used to the value of debts being wiped out by price rises, but real interest rates have turned sharply positive, often well into triple digits.
The cocktail has pushed some 5.8mn people to fall behind on payments, almost a third of all borrowers.

Personal debts have become a flashpoint in anger over the uneven impact of Milei’s free-market reforms. Argentines have seen salaries shrink or stall since the inflation crisis in 2023 as industries including construction, manufacturing and retail suffer a slowdown, even as exporting sectors such as agriculture and energy boom.
“There is [economic] growth, but people don’t feel it,” said Nery Persichini, head of research at broker GMA Capital. “A lot of people are having a bad time in this transition.”

Argentina’s fragmented leftwing Peronist opposition has unified around the debt issue, with its leaders repeatedly accusing Milei of forcing people “to get into debt to survive”. Labour unions marched in Buenos Aires last week to demand relief.

The president’s office hit back on Monday, saying the figures “do not show a crisis situation” and that arrears “are trending towards a decrease” after June data showed the share of loans in arrears had stabilised since May.

His officials say the surge in delinquencies is a temporary consequence of a long-overdue expansion of Argentina’s private credit market, which at 12 per cent of GDP remains tiny compared to neighbouring countries. It was worsened, they add, by a sharp increase in interest rates last year as lenders shielded themselves from market volatility ahead of midterm elections.

Milei himself has shown little sympathy for debtors. “Did anyone put a gun to their head to do it?” he said in a television interview this month, describing arrears as “a problem between private actors”.
But economists say the scale of the phenomenon is a problem for Milei, 14 months out from his bid for re-election.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
“With so many people involved, this stops being a microeconomic issue and threatens to become a macroeconomic one,” said Amílcar Collante, founder of consultancy Profit.
Milei’s government views private credit as one of its biggest levers to lift consumer spending and economic activity, which are both growing more slowly than his government expected.
“It’s not clear that credit can help with activity when you have so many people unable to borrow because of unpaid debts,” Collante said.

Economy minister Luis Caputo is seeking alternative ways to expand the credit market, including by allowing banks to loan out 15 per cent of their dollar deposits to companies — something that has been largely banned since a 2001 economic crash.

Argentina’s notoriously volatile economy has long dissuaded banks from lending to the private sector. Instead, they earned easy money from national governments, which in recent years issued huge volumes of interest-paying debt to fund spending.
Milei’s austerity has changed that, encouraging banks to seek businesses and individuals as customers.

But individuals have found it hard to anticipate their capacity to repay, as the decline in inflation slowed the pace of salary increases and Milei scrapped subsidies for gas, electricity and transport.

“You take out a loan thinking you can pay it back,” said Oriana Fernández, a 24-year-old clothing company analyst. She owes about $3,300 on a credit card with a 132 per cent interest rate, after spending $1,600 last year to secure an apartment for her and her son when she split with her partner.

Her employer, struggling to compete as Milei relaxes Argentina’s import restrictions, had increased her salary by only 20 per cent in the past 18 months, said Fernández, a member of Organised Debtors, a collective supporting people in arrears.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The surge in bad loans has stoked anger at digital wallet providers, which are hugely popular in Argentina. More than 32 per cent of credit to individuals from fintechs and other non-bank lenders is overdue, according to Equilibra.

Protesters last week accused Milei of being “an accomplice” to “usury” by fintechs. “They are charging 200 per cent interest, which is usury when you consider how little capacity people have to repay,” said Luci Cavallero, founder of Movida Ciudad, a community action group in Buenos Aires.

Mariano Biocca, head of Argentina’s fintech chamber, said digital wallets must set higher interest rates than banks because they deal with higher-risk borrowers, and that fintech loans made up a small fraction of total overdue debt.

“This is a learning process,” Biocca said, adding that “all credit providers have been slowing down this year as they recalibrate their decision-making”. Central bank data shows the credit offering to individuals has barely expanded since late 2025.
Milei has ruled out government-backed debt relief, though Caputo said last month that lenders had their own plans “to refinance debts at longer terms and lower rates”.

Economists are watching such efforts closely as Argentina moves towards the 2027 presidential elections. The stalling economy has weighed on Milei’s support this year, with 38 per cent of respondents approving of his government, according to pollster Casa Tres.

“When you don’t have genuine spending power in people’s pockets because of smaller disposable incomes, you need the motor of credit to drive consumer spending,” said Persichini of GMA Capital. “Right now, that motor is off.”

/content/6b355049-3122-4167-8a8a-ce37da7.title: Institutional investors back Blackstone and KKR funds for wealthy individuals
articleContent: Institutional investors are putting money into Blackstone and KKR vehicles set up to woo wealthy individuals, a move by the traditional backers of private equity that could ultimately upend the sector’s traditional 10-year fund model.

Evergreen funds, which allow investors to withdraw funds at regular intervals rather than lock up their capital for long periods, have become increasingly common as a way to make private equity and credit accessible to wealthy individuals.
But the funds, which tend to charge lower fees and target lower returns than the industry’s traditional closed-end funds, have also started to draw in institutional investors.

Blackstone’s evergreen funds for individuals had raised a “small percentage” from institutions, the firm’s head of wealth Joan Solotar told the FT. Interest had increased in the past year, she added. “It will continue to evolve and grow.”
KKR’s head of client solutions, Eric Mogelof, said it had recently launched institutional share classes in its buyout, credit and infrastructure evergreens to meet “growing demand”.
The budding interest among large investors in evergreen funds has raised questions about how the new structures could accelerate fundamental changes under way in private markets.

Listed private markets firms such as Blackstone, KKR and Apollo have increasingly targeted retail investors to help turbocharge their growth and diversify their revenues away from unpredictable performance fees.
At the same time many institutional investors have been reluctant to make fresh commitments to the sector at a time when firms have struggled to sell investments and return cash.

Pension plans and endowments lock up cash for a decade in traditional private funds, but some predict that the flurry of evergreens recently launched by the world’s biggest asset managers will fuel a race to the bottom on fees.

Increasing competition for deals in recent years had left many funds offering “beta” returns that track rather than beat the wider market, said Patrick Dwyer of NewEdge Wealth. The increasing “commoditisation” of the sector meant that many institutions would start choosing lower-fee evergreens with regular chances to withdraw, he added.
After making a commitment at the start of a traditional fund’s life, backers must manage that cash themselves until the manager gradually calls it down upon finding investment opportunities.

Evergreens, meanwhile, take all of an investor’s commitment as cash on day one, removing the need for complex cash flow management that small organisations can find cumbersome. The funds’ need to keep cash on hand for redemptions generally leads to lower returns.

“We are at the beginning of a trend, but it’s going to continue to happen as the evergreen market evolves,” said Hugh MacArthur, chair of private equity at consultants Bain & Company. “Institutions are going to want the same . . . conveniences as individuals.”

The buyout sector’s struggles to sell companies and return cash to backers since interest rate rises in 2022 would trigger many institutions to choose evergreen funds offering regular liquidity, he added.

Solotar of Blackstone said big institutions with staff to manage complex cash flows would still choose traditional funds, and that some were backing both types of vehicle. The UK’s Universities Superannuation Scheme was one example, people familiar with the matter said.

In 2022 the University of California invested on favourable terms in Blackstone’s evergreen property fund to help the fund meet a spate of redemption requests. Other pension plans have in recent years backed real estate or infrastructure evergreens.

/content/3b7ac1fe-4761-4b4a-8fff-95c8c28.title: ‘Embarrassing’: US officials recoil from Trump’s Canada attacks
articleContent: The Trump administration’s attacks on Canada have sparked a backlash among former US national security officials and Republicans, including claims Washington is “embarrassing” the US and demeaning a long-term ally.

Donald Trump and lieutenants have repeatedly aimed barbs at Canada’s military and sovereignty in recent months — but the broadsides escalated after trade talks between the countries collapsed on Friday, exposing cracks in the president’s own movement just months ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump on Tuesday said that he wanted to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, because “we don’t expect to [be] doing much business with Ontario any longer”. The comment came a day after Ontario’s premier Doug Ford called Trump “a loser”.

US vice-president JD Vance piled on the insults during a speech on Monday in Maine, which borders Canada — described as a “state” by Vance in an attempted joke — and has a blockbuster toss-up race for a US Senate seat.

“Canada is a country that has underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by” the US, Vance told the crowd.
Vance’s claims about Canada’s defence echoed comments by US transportation secretary Sean Duffy, who told Fox News that Canada was “a country that doesn’t have a military”.
Former US military leaders reacted badly. Canadian troops have fought alongside the US in several American military conflicts.

“Mr secretary, please stop embarrassing us,” said Ben Hodges, the former commanding general of the US Army in Europe, referring to Duffy. “I served in Kandahar, Afghanistan in 2009-2010 alongside Canadian soldiers. They were skilled, courageous and effective. We were lucky to be on the same side with them.”

Nato-member Canada is among the US’s closest military partners, with the two sharing the North American Aerospace Defense Command (Norad), a mutual defence organisation. Canada deployed about 40,000 troops to Afghanistan over 12 years, suffering 158 deaths.

Karen Gibson, the former intelligence director at US Central Command, praised Canadian forces for their work alongside Americans in Afghanistan, Iraq and Kuwait. “We were stronger for their presence,” she told the FT, adding that the Norad partnership was “vital”.

One retired admiral, who served alongside Canadian special forces, told the FT that Canada’s “professional, competent forces” had added “much-needed capacity” to US war efforts including in Afghanistan.

“Fact: Canada has a brave and professional military. It has deployed into combat with us many times, including D-Day. Canadian troops, under my Nato command, faced intense fire in Afghanistan where many were killed in action. I honor their memory and salute them,” wrote James Stavridis, a retired US admiral.

Washington slapped new tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods on Saturday hours after negotiations collapsed in acrimony. On Monday, Trump said he would increase levies on Canadian cars and automotive parts to 50 per cent. Canada was set to announce its retaliatory measures later on Tuesday.
The war of words has intensified as the US has escalated its trade conflict.
Vance rekindled the White House’s position that Canada should become the US’s 51st state during his speech in Maine.
“We have to remember Canada is a state. Sorry, Freudian slip,” Vance said. “That was actually an accident,” he contended.
On Monday Trump called Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney “Governor” in a social media post — an insult he also used to denigrate Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau.
Doug Ford, the pugnacious premier of Ontario — home to Canada’s auto-manufacturing hub, which has for decades been closely integrated with American supply chains — told Trump to “kiss my ass”.
Republicans fighting for re-election in battleground states that could suffer from Trump’s imposition of new border taxes on consumer goods have also balked at the president’s latest trade war.
Susan Collins, a Republican US senator trying to hold her seat in Maine, warned that Trump’s new levies would bring economic pain to Americans.
“I still think imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake” because they will increase costs for Mainers, Collins told reporters on Monday.

“We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it . . . that increases the cost of eating, building homes, and our best known products”, she added.
Collins did not attend Vance’s speech.

Scott Brown, a Republican vying for a US Senate seat in New Hampshire, which also borders Canada, told Semafor on Monday that “there’s gotta be a better way to negotiate or negotiate an agreement with our neighbor”.

/content/7ced71c2-03b8-4569-a68d-14624a7.title: Canada announces $20bn retaliatory tariffs as US trade war escalates
articleContent: Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs of up to 50 per cent on US$20bn worth of US imports a day after Donald Trump said he would raise duties on Canadian cars, in the latest salvo of an escalating trade war between the two neighbours.

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne on Tuesday issued a 99-page list of hundreds of US goods that will face increased levies in Canada from September 8 including steel, dairy products and agricultural equipment.
“When the US asked too much and offered too little, we chose to stand up for Canadians,” said Champagne, referring to the trade talks that collapsed on Friday.
Canada’s move follows months of tortured trade talks between Washington and Ottawa and comes as the US president steps up rhetorical attacks on the US’s northern neighbour.

But the trade tensions come at a perilous moment for the US economy, with the White House battling stubborn inflation and increasing voter unhappiness over its handling of the economy weeks before crucial midterm elections.
Canada will impose counter-tariffs of 15, 25 or 50 per cent on US products, matching the rates applied to the same categories of Canadian exports by Washington.
Trade analysts said that while Canada’s response was proportional, the fresh duties would create more uncertainty for American and Canadian businesses.

“This is a standard tit-for-tat and classic proportional response,” said Edward Alden, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, who said the measures seemed designed to reset negotiations.
Ottawa also on Tuesday announced a new $5.5bn package to bail out Canadian businesses and workers hurt by Trump’s barrage of levies.

Champagne said: “Our dollar-for-dollar, rate-for-rate counter-tariffs as well as a multibillion-dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families and businesses as we build a stronger, more resilient and more diversified Canadian economy.”
In a press conference, industry minister Mélanie Joly said the federal government would be “flexible and adaptable” to the needs of Canadian businesses.
She also urged Canadians to pitch in by supporting local businesses that will bear the brunt of the latest US measures.
“When you choose a Canadian product, you’re not only putting pressure on the US, you’re protecting Canadian jobs,” she said.
Trump launched tariffs targeting $20bn worth of Canadian goods that went into effect on Saturday after Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the US late the previous night.
The US president on Monday said he would increase tariffs on Canadian cars and automotive parts beginning on January 1, and on Tuesday he threatened to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”.
Recommended
Derek Nighbor, president of the Forest Products Association of Canada, said the country’s forestry sector had been one of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs.
“Duties and tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of our products now range from 25 per cent to 85 per cent,” he told the FT.
“The addition of Section 338 tariffs over the weekend make immediate federal support essential to help keep facilities operating and employees connected to their places of work.”
Robert Wolfe, professor emeritus at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, said Canada’s response was “the minimum they could do”.
“They can’t not respond with what Trump is doing,” Wolfe said. “They’re reciprocal tariffs,” he added, referring to the name Trump gave to his steep levies first issued in April last year.

/content/9a6947bf-9d4e-4489-80b9-2178ea6.title: Alphaville. Nvidia’s $200bn ‘balance sheet-as-a-service’
articleContent: Hundred-billion-dollar customer subsidies might not look like much, for a $5tn cash machine, but they’re still enough to worry about, according to a note on Nvidia from Morgan Stanley’s corporate credit team.

Initiating coverage with a “neutral” — which we all know what is actually code for — analysts Lindsay Tyler and Nishant Satyam praise how Nvidia “turns balance-sheet strength into a strategic AI financing tool”, but argue that “the tail remains too early stage, opaque, and sizeable to step in”. Because:
Conventional leverage increasingly understates the [Nvidia] credit story as ecosystem support sits in contingent, contractual, and potentially off-balance-sheet forms.
They dub phenomenon “balance-sheet-as-a-service.” The big question Morgan Stanley’s analysts seek to answer is how much of Nvidia’s support packages and lease commitments should be treated as debt.

Prompting the question is Nvidia’s announcement this month of “repeatable financing platform” agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise more than $500bn for AI infrastructure build-outs.

On the company blog, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the fundraisings were designed to address concerns about circular financing. Bringing in the big guns marked “the beginning of an open capital market for AI infrastructure”, where Nvidia would pay only a “residual-value support mechanism for up to 25 per cent of an opportunity”.

It doesn’t take an analyst to work out that 25 per cent of >$500bn is still a lot. But with the capital market for AI infrastructure currently just a collection of memorandums-of-understanding, estimating Nvidia’s potential credit exposure takes some guesswork.

The Morgan Stanley analysts use as their template the $35bn chip-lease agreement the bank organised for Broadcom to lease its Google co-designed tensor processing units to Anthropic. In effect, Broadcom keeps the expense off its balance sheet by selling the chips to a private credit vehicle, funded using debt raised by Apollo and Blackstone, most of which it backstops:

Based on Nvidia signing 15 similar fundraisings by the end of 2028, and taking into account drawdowns and amortisation, its tail risk exposure would peak at nearly $90bn shortly after that date, Morgan Stanley estimates. Company disclosures will be limited, however, and rating agencies have already indicated a preference to view Nvidia’s whole ca $125bn of financing structures as debt-like.
Nvidia’s individual arrangements with customers are the analysts’ bigger concern, partly because so little is known about them.

In a blog last month, Nvidia said it was introducing a “revenue-sharing and credit-support model” aimed at expanding chip access beyond the hyperscalers. The best guess among industry watchers is that Nvidia will offer neocloud providers a guaranteed floor on their per-hour GPU rental pricing in return for a share of revenue above that level, on top of standard product revenue.
As Morgan Stanley’s equity team wrote in a recent note:

Our sense is that NVIDIA believes that 1) hyperscalers are not investing enough to keep up with token demand because of fcf concerns, 2) hyperscalers can’t get land power shell outside the US and are increasingly getting pressure in the US so the world needs new spenders, and 3) the structure here will drive tens of billions of annuity revenue with limited downside. Of course, the more cynical view is it is simply creating artificial demand from customers without the scale to use asic or AMD, but it only works if compute demand is ahead of supply.

Guaranteeing minimum revenue helps solve the problem of relying on short-term leases to service long-term infrastructure debt. Nvidia’s backstop means the neocloud operator can pay for its build-out using money raised at near-investment grade.
But customer backstops won’t do much to ease worries about circular financing, as the bank’s credit analysts illustrate:
[enlarge]
Revenue guarantees, whether or not they’re triggered, also create contingent obligations.
Assuming Nvidia’s backstops 5GW of revenue-generating capacity for customers, there’s a $81bn pre-tax contingent obligation by 2028.

Such a liability would be a big step up from Nvidia’s $6.3bn agreement with CoreWeave to buy its unused capacity up to an estimated 500MW, announced in September 2025. But in a sprint to unlock AI infrastructure funding, who knows how concentrated the risk might become across a few connected counterparties, and how shonky the underlying customer credit quality might get.

In total, by the 2028 year-end, Nvidia will be carrying an all-in credit exposure of approximately $200bn, around $170bn of which will be adjustments and contingent obligations related to the customer backstops, Morgan Stanley credit analysts estimate.

Not surprisingly, since this is Morgan Stanley, it’s not a Margot Robbie In a Bath Tub analysis. Nvidia’s balance sheet still appears bulletproof on an all-in basis: gross debt leverage is only 0.4 times, rising to just 0.7 times assuming growth plateaus in 2028. Peak-level debt would have to at least double again, approximately, to put Nvidia on the threshold of an S&P credit rating downgrade:
But Tyler and Satyam start on a “neutral” recommendation because you’ll sleep better by not getting involved.

Be patient, they advise, because right now there are no good ways to estimate tail risks; not when there’s more than $1tn of vendor circular opaque financing pulsing through “creative structures in the ecosystem”.

/content/33304634-1594-487c-9031-5fdf7ad.title: Deloitte to pay $21.5mn in Trump DEI crackdown
articleContent: Deloitte will pay the US government $21.5mn to settle claims that its diversity practices were discriminatory and broke federal contracting laws as the Trump administration continues its crackdown on corporate hiring practices.

The accounting and consulting firm set race- and sex-based goals for the make-up of its workforce and tied tens of thousands of dollars of partner remuneration to achieving the targets, in contravention of promises that it did not discriminate in hiring and promotions, the US Department of Justice said on Tuesday.

Deloitte denied the claims but agreed to pay $10mn in restitution and a further $11.5mn to settle the matter. The firm is one of the biggest consultants to the US government, and its contracts stipulate that it complies with anti-discrimination practices.
The justice department contended that Deloitte’s diversity, equity and inclusion efforts layered costs on to the business that were passed on to the government in higher fees.
“Government contractors cannot reward or penalise employees based on race or sex, and labelling the practice DEI does not make it lawful,” said US attorney-general Todd Blanche.

The settlement under the False Claims Act comes three months after Deloitte rival IBM agreed to pay $17.1mn to settle similar allegations. US companies have faced a ferocious backlash against DEI practices during President Donald Trump’s second term in office, leading many to row back public commitments and downplay previous initiatives.
Deloitte has stopped publishing annual DEI transparency reports, in which it had set out goals to increase the proportion of Black and Hispanic staff and women in its workforce.
It was one of several professional services businesses targeted by the American Alliance for Equal Rights, a group set up by conservative campaigner Edward Blum.
Blum in 2023 won a decades-long battle to end racially conscious admissions at US universities, and sued Deloitte on the government’s behalf. The AAER will get a $4.3mn cut of the settlement.

Business units within Deloitte received monthly summaries tracking progress against demographic goals, the government alleged, according to Tuesday’s settlement. Evaluations of partners and other managers were also partially based on contributions to helping Deloitte achieve the goals. About 150 senior figures had their pay tied to the progress.

“Today’s settlement is yet another example of this department’s commitment to eliminating woke, unconstitutional practices from American workplaces,” associate attorney-general Stanley Woodward Jr said on Tuesday.

The settlement document states that it was “neither an admission of liability by Deloitte nor a concession by the United States that its claims are not well founded. Deloitte denies that it engaged in the [conduct claimed] and denies the allegations in the civil action.”

The firm added: “We are pleased to have resolved this matter to avoid the cost and distraction of protracted litigation, allowing us to remain focused on attracting and developing exceptional talent with the skills and capabilities our clients rely on every day.”

/content/303655df-662d-4d40-8a5d-9ced4da.title: Macquarie dumps KPMG after Australian data scandal
articleContent: Macquarie Group has dropped KPMG as its new auditor after questioning the Big Four firm’s culture and ability to conduct the work following a damaging data-sharing scandal.

KPMG Australia won Macquarie’s audit contract, which generates almost A$75mn (US$49mn) a year in fees and is the most lucrative in Australia, from PwC late last year. It was due to take on the work in 2027 after a lengthy handover period.

However, KPMG’s Australian unit has been in turmoil for months after allegations about the misuse of confidential documents by senior members of its audit team to win new business, as well as the mishandling of a whistleblower complaint into the issue.
The upheaval has triggered a freeze on new work, the departure of many of KPMG’s most senior audit partners and executives, and gruelling Senate hearings into the scandal.

Last month, Macquarie said it would review its decision to switch to KPMG in light of the scandal. It made the unexpected decision to retain PwC — its auditor since the early 1990s — following a board meeting on Wednesday.

It said the decision followed the scrutiny being applied to KPMG’s Australian business. Macquarie added that the move also came after its own enquiries into the auditor’s capacity to complete the work in light of audit partner departures as well as the “nature and impact of ongoing issues” at the firm.

It said in a statement that the boards of Macquarie Group and Macquarie Bank held “concerns in respect of KPMG Australia and its audit practice in two of the key criteria considered in the audit tender completed in late 2025, namely capacity to deliver the audit given several key members of the proposed KPMG Australia audit team have departed; and culture, including a culture that transparently discloses issues”.
John Sams, who was appointed as chief executive of KPMG Australia last month, said Macquarie’s decision underscored the importance of the “sweeping programme of change under way” across the firm.
“The consequences of our past failings are real. Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time,” he said.

Macquarie was itself drawn into the KPMG scandal owing to the involvement of Michelle Hinchliffe, a former lead audit partner at the Big Four firm’s UK unit who sits on the Macquarie board, in the early stages of the audit tender.

The asset manager has defended its tender process. Glenn Stevens, its chair and the former governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, was called to appear at a Senate committee when he argued that the global scale and complexity of its contract restricted its choice of auditor to the Big Four owing to their global reach.

“That’s the reality that we face. Obviously, it’s really important that those four be capable and ethical. That’s the world that we’re in,” he told senators this month.

The switch provides an unexpected boon for PwC Australia. It was forced to restructure in 2023 after the internal leaking of confidential government information about tax laws led to the suspension of senior partners, intense political scrutiny and a substantial loss of work.
PwC said: “It is a privilege to continue supporting Macquarie and delivering audits of the highest quality. We also note this remains a challenging time for our industry.”

/content/04bad7f3-1b5d-4982-9967-229886b.title: Insurers pile into deals allowing banks to offload default risk
articleContent: Banks nearly doubled the risk they offloaded to insurers through a booming securitisation trade last year, as the lenders sought to free up more capital for lending.

In 2025, insurers signed up to cover the risk of default on €4.7bn in synthetic risk transfers, up from €2.7bn in 2024, according to new survey data from the International Association of Credit Portfolio Managers.

Insurers remain a fraction of the booming market for European banks’ credit risk, which last year shifted risks worth €579bn in SRTs to investors including hedge funds and private credit funds, according to Barclays analysts.

Banks use the structures to offload the default risk on a pool of loans to outside investors in exchange for a fee. Those investors are then usually on the hook for losses up to an agreed cap, and the banks secure more favourable capital treatment from regulators, which means they can then lend more.
But insurers have the advantage that they can cover these risks on an “unfunded” basis, meaning that, unlike hedge funds, they are not required to set aside money to cover losses.

Whereas hedge funds and other investors typically deposit collateral in an account for the duration of an SRT deal, insurers can rely on their credit ratings and existing balance sheets to manage these risks.

The property and casualty insurers offering these arrangements typically also cover corporate policyholders against risks ranging from hurricanes to cyber attacks. As a result, regulators have allowed them to take on exposure to largely uncorrelated risks, such as bank defaults, relatively cheaply.
Munich Re, The Fidelis Partnership, and AIG-backed insurer Convex are among the speciality groups offering SRT coverage.
Between 2019 and 2025 banks shifted €10.9bn of credit risk to insurers through SRTs, said the IACPM, mostly corresponding to mezzanine debt from loan pools.

SRTs have come in for scrutiny from some regulators and analysts due to their similarity to credit default swaps, which brought large insurers such as AIG to the brink of collapse during the global financial crisis of 2008.

“Credit default swaps are unfunded credit protection,” said Monsur Hussain, head of markets research at Fitch Ratings. “It’s essentially the same technology” as SRTs, he said, but added that “AIG were doing it at a volume that is not being witnessed for European insurers”.
Hussain added that Fitch had raised concerns over banks’ exposure to risks in the event that insurers or other counterparties stopped providing SRT coverage.

“The concern is, if there’s an expectation with the bank that they can roll these agreements, but suddenly the counterparties — hedge funds, insurance companies — say they are unable to provide that protection any longer,” he said.
“If for whatever reason the participants in the market are unable to provide or roll over the protection, the banks might be forced to deleverage, because suddenly the capital requirements go up.”

/content/c57569fb-c1ee-476a-aa31-d402e2f.title: Obituary. Dolly Parton, singer-songwriter, 1946-2026
articleContent: Dolly Parton was at once larger than life and down to earth. The Nashville star, who has died aged 80, was a vision of fabulous folksiness with her blonde wigs, rhinestones and dazzling smile. She wrote songs in industrial quantities, about 3,000 in her estimation, but performed them with a very human wit and warmth. With more than 100mn record sales to her name and a renown stretching far beyond the boundaries of her genre, she ranks among the greatest artists in the history of country music.

She was born in rural Tennessee in 1946, at the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains. Her father was a sharecropper who later became a tobacco farmer. Her mother had 12 children, including Parton, by the age of 35. It was an impoverished upbringing. According to Parton, her penniless father paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. “I have often joked that I have been raking in the dough ever since,” she wrote in her autobiography, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business.

There was neither self-pity nor selfishness in her passage from rags to riches. She sang about being mocked by schoolmates for wearing a coat made from scraps of fabric in “Coat of Many Colors”. “I couldn’t understand it, for I felt I was rich,” Parton sang in the 1971 signature song. “And I told them of the love my momma sewed in every stitch.” At this point in the song, a key change lifts us up too.

She could dole out schmaltz with the best of them, although she was a sophisticated singer and songwriter too. Drawn to music from a young age, she was brought up amid the music of church and family gatherings rather than records or radio. After graduating from high school, she left home for Nashville in 1964. Another autobiographical song, “The Letter”, evokes the small-town girl’s first weeks in Music City, singing on morning television shows and writing hits for other acts.

Her first country hit as a recording artist came in 1967 with the single “Dumb Blonde”. “This dumb blonde ain’t nobody’s fool,” she sang. It was penned by another Nashville songwriter, but the mix of self-mockery and defiance was typical of Parton. Country music’s tradition of strong womanhood allowed a certain degree of challenge to its even more powerful culture of sexism. Parton was audacious yet also astute in testing the limits that she faced.

Initially, her extravagantly quivering voice was divisive. “I just don’t think the girl can sing,” a record executive told Nashville veteran Porter Wagoner when he proposed teaming with Parton as a duo in 1967. Wagoner insisted, and the partnership was a success. It provided the platform for her solo career to blossom in the early 1970s with hits such as “Coat of Many Colors”.

In 1974 she released her 13th solo album, Jolene. Its title track highlighted Parton’s storytelling and role-playing talents, a mini-masterpiece in which she sings the part of a woman pleading with an alpha rival not to take her man. The album also contains “I Will Always Love You”, written as a farewell to her mentor. It was given a powerhouse pop-soul revision by Whitney Houston in 1992, one of the best-selling singles ever.

The untutored twang of Parton’s vocal tone carried memories of the Appalachian region where she was raised, a rural heartland for the bluegrass music that preceded the Nashville country machine. But Parton was not a purist. She crossed over into the mainstream pop charts with 1977’s adult-contemporary classic “Here You Come Again”, written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, notables from New York’s Brill Building song factory.
Recommended

“It costs me a lot of money to look this cheap,” she liked to quip of her look, an exuberant cartoon of Southern femininity involving high heels, sequins and figure-hugging dresses that turned her bust into an American icon. She claimed to have been inspired by a local “lady of the night” whom she saw while growing up. But her diva appearance was crafted in the 1970s with the help of celebrated designer Bob Mackie, who also costumed Liza Minnelli and Barbra Streisand.

A move into films with the 1980 comedy 9 to 5 sealed her superstar status. Its theme song provided her with another imperishable hit, a boogying number about female office drudgery in which she ingeniously created a beat from the click-clack of acrylic fingernails hitting typewriter keys. In her own working life, Parton was not prepared to take dictation from the men who ran the music industry. Elvis Presley’s grasping manager Colonel Tom Parker was sent packing when he demanded that she hand over half the publishing rights to “I Will Always Love You” if Presley covered the song.

In Nashville, she was nicknamed the Iron Butterfly. She cultivated her image assiduously, but with good humour and authenticity rather than cynical self-branding. In 1986, she founded a theme park in Tennessee called Dollywood. Her many charitable ventures included a literacy foundation that had distributed more than 300mn books to children across the English-speaking world by 2025.

While not departing from country’s values of God, flag and family, Parton was a freethinker by conventional Nashville standards. She supported gay rights such as same-sex marriage and took pride in her LGBT+ following. Her musical eclecticism led from the traditional bluegrass of her 1999 album The Grass Is Blue, which won a Grammy award, to a bravura switch into rock music with 2023’s Rockstar.

She was married to businessman Carl Dean from 1966 to his death in 2025, and marked his passing with a song, “If You Hadn’t Been There”. Their time together was shrouded in privacy, the unseen backdrop to Parton’s expansive public life.
“If you become a star you make a pact with the world that you belong with them,” she once said. Few have honoured that pact as magnificently as her.

/content/2fe2913f-24b7-4074-9278-3253b5b.title: Berlin’s defence push draws global groups to set up shop in Germany
articleContent: Germany is becoming a magnet for international defence groups as Berlin’s military spending boom prompts companies from around the world to establish a presence in the country.

Aerospace and defence companies from Europe and beyond have set up offices in Germany over the past 12 months, including the Norwegian space group Kongsberg, the Finnish satellite intelligence start-up Iceye and the South Korean defence giant Hanwha Aerospace.

Australia’s Electro Optic Systems, which makes high-precision lasers that can neutralise hostile drones and engage in space warfare, plans to go a step further by relocating its headquarters from Canberra to Europe.

“All the significant future budget increases in defence will happen in Europe, because of geopolitics,” chief executive Andreas Schwer told the FT. “We strongly intend to move our headquarters from Australia to central Europe. We have not decided upon the final destination, but among different options the Netherlands and Germany are quite likely candidates.”

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has triggered a significant change in Germany’s approach to its military, after decades when the country spent as little as 1 per cent of GDP on defence.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz exempted defence from Germany’s strict rules on borrowing after winning elections last year, as he pledged to make the Bundeswehr the strongest conventional army in Europe. The EU’s most populous country has since budgeted more than €700bn for defence over the coming five years — a figure that has caught the attention of global defence firms.

“Everybody wants a piece of the pie,” said Nils Lange, project manager in the Berlin office of advisory firm Rasmussen Global, which works with international companies on navigating the German market.
“Germany has suddenly become an interesting market, not just for selling to the German armed forces, but also as a defence-industrial hub for the rest of Europe.”

Alex Wong, global chief strategy officer at Hanwha Group, said that his company put an office in Germany because the scale of the opportunity “required a permanent presence [and] required us to hire individuals very familiar with the German defence market to push the strategy forward”.

The trend of establishing a local footprint was also part of a broader pattern worldwide that had seen governments pushing for more “localisation and domestication” to reduce the risk that conflict or geopolitical tension could jeopardise access to crucial weapons, he added.

While Hanwha had long exported to international markets, Wong said, it was now getting inquiries to move its capacity to locations around the world “so we can begin to speed up production for allies and partners”.
Lange said that German officials preferred, when possible, not to procure entire systems — such as tanks or warships — from non-European companies that competed with German industry.
But he said that they were open to foreign companies being “plugged into the supply chains of established manufacturers here” to help ease capacity challenges.

Foreign companies can also tap the booming German market through joint ventures. Rheinmetall, the German tank and ammunition maker, has signed a flurry of deals with international groups to offer foreign technology combined with local production and political knowhow.

They include a plan to make low-cost cruise missiles with the Dutch start-up Destinus and medium- and long-range air defence with South Korea’s LIG Defense & Aerospace, as well as a partnership with US-based satellite imagery provider Vantor. Rheinmetall has also paired up with the Australian division of Boeing to offer an unmanned fighter aircraft made by the US aviation giant to the German air force.

/content/557217e6-f62b-4fb6-a451-533e43c.title: Hyundai bets on US hybrid boom to take on Toyota
articleContent: Hyundai will take on Toyota with a big hybrid push in the US as the world’s third-largest carmaker aims to capitalise on surging demand amid sliding electric vehicle sales in America.

The South Korean group unveiled an aggressive product roadmap of more than 100 new launches and refreshes by 2030, of which 58 will be in North America where it expects hybrids to account for more than half its sales.
“North America is where our hybrid story became a scale story,” said José Muñoz, chief executive of Hyundai Motor, at its investor day on Wednesday.

Hyundai’s hybrid sales in the US rose 71 per cent year on year during the second quarter. The popularity of hybrids, due to higher fuel prices, has caught out Detroit’s Big Three carmakers, which offer few such models in the US.
The group also plans to enter 18 new segments including mid-size pick-ups in a direct challenge to Ford, Toyota and General Motors in one of the most lucrative US segments.
To address plummeting EV sales in the US following the cancellation of tax credits, Hyundai will launch range-extended EVs in the first half of next year.
Its Santa Fe range-extended EV, which has a small engine that acts only as a generator to top up the battery, will target more than 600 miles of total range and will be built at its Alabama plant.
Hyundai’s heavy focus on the US comes as it faces intense competition from BYD and Chinese rivals in other markets such as Europe.
Despite its ambitious product plans, Hyundai shares fell more than 3 per cent in Seoul. However, the stock has gained about 36 per cent this year.

“Hyundai has no other choice but to make a bigger push into the hybrid market to protect its margins and market share in the US with the hybrid market getting bigger there,” said Lee Hang-koo, a researcher at the Korea Automotive Technology Institute. “But it is struggling to compete with Chinese rivals in non-US EV markets including Europe and emerging markets with higher growth rates.”

Hyundai also plans to increase production capacity by 1.27mn vehicles by 2027, including 500,000 in North America. It aims to increase local parts sourcing in the US from 60 per cent to 80 per cent to address Donald Trump’s tariffs on auto imports.
Hyundai, which bought Boston Dynamics in 2021, also plans to compete with the likes of Tesla in humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles.
The company said it expected to produce Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robot in 2028 at its Georgia plant with 30,000 units of annual capacity.
Tesla has said it aims to begin mass production of its Optimus robot by the end of this year with a longer-term target of producing 1mn units per year.
Lee also said it remained unclear if Hyundai could secure major buyers for its robots with China dominating global humanoid robot production.
“It remains questionable where Hyundai can sell 5,000 robots although 25,000 units will be deployed in its US plant, as China makes much cheaper and highly capable robots,” said Lee.

/content/aa7ba671-8175-4b53-b6a5-28803a8.title: China warns US it could retaliate over Iran sanctions
articleContent: Beijing has warned the US that it will retaliate if Chinese companies are included in any significant expansion of the Trump administration’s new secondary sanctions relating to Iran.
The measures unveiled on Monday by US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent targeted companies based in Hong Kong and mainland China but stopped short of listing large Chinese financial institutions.

Any serious increase in US sanctions on China, which buys 90 per cent of Iran’s oil, would risk exploding the relationship only a month before presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet in Washington.

The summit is seen as crucial to the world economy, with the leaders expected to discuss extending a one-year truce in their trade war that they agreed in October and which was cemented by a cordial visit to Beijing by Trump in May.

“China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests,” a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday in response to questions about US secondary sanctions on Iran.
“China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” they said.
“The pressing task is to facilitate de-escalation of the situation and return to dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible,” they added.
While China’s large state-owned refiners largely comply with sanctions on Iranian crude, Beijing allows private sector refiners known as “teapots” to import and process oil from the country.
Recommended
The US imposed sanctions on some of these refiners earlier this year but China ordered domestic companies not to comply.

China has set up an increasingly strident anti-sanctions regime that includes countermeasures against foreign individuals and organisations that assist with foreign restrictions on Chinese companies and supply chains.

Any attempt by the US to aggressively expand a secondary sanctions regime on Iran to Chinese companies would risk retaliation from Beijing, which last year showed that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals essential to high-tech production.
“We have to wait and see whether this is just bluffing or [the US is] seriously thinking about putting secondary sanctions on China,” said Wang Dong, a senior scholar at Peking University.
“If they do, then of course China will absolutely defend its national interest . . . we already did that during round one last year,” he added.
He said Washington was trying to “shift responsibility on to others and blame China for its own failure”.

But Zhu Feng, an international relations expert at Nanjing University, said that behind the scenes, China was deeply interested in encouraging the warring parties in the US-Iran conflict to find a solution.
He noted that the continued restrictions on shipping through the crucial Strait of Hormuz due to the conflict are straining the entire global economy.

“From a Chinese perspective, we don’t want to get involved in a US-Iranian fight,” he said. “On the other hand, we are also very highly aware that if the Strait of Hormuz dilemma continues, it will also be more dangerous for China. China’s main oil imports come from the Middle East, not from Iran but from Saudi Arabia and Iraq.”
In recent days, Xi has met King Abdullah II of Jordan while foreign minister Wang Yi has met his Kuwaiti counterpart, with Iran and the war in Gaza discussed in both meetings.
“So China’s message to Tehran is very clear — we hope the peace talks will continue,” said Zhu.

/content/b6009dd2-7e97-4bbc-941d-cd0b8fc.title: Can Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ force Iran to capitulate?
articleContent: As Donald Trump sought to raise pressure on Iran, he vowed to impose “the highest level” economic sanctions to force Tehran to submit to US demands for a new nuclear deal.
“Today’s action sends a critical message: the United States no longer makes empty threats,” Trump said.

But that was May 2018, when the US president in his first term declared he was withdrawing from the 2015 nuclear accord between Tehran, Washington and other world powers. The announcement marked the beginning of Trump’s “maximum pressure” campaign, which imposed hundreds of swingeing sanctions on Iran and targeted entities trading with the Islamic republic.

Now, eight years on, Trump is threatening Iran with “economic D-day” — what his Treasury secretary Scott Bessent described as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.

After six months of war, it is Washington’s latest attempt to force the regime to cave to its demands and lift its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz. As with Trump’s previous campaign, it aims to further isolate Iran and cut it off from trading partners with the threat of secondary sanctions.
Yet “maximum pressure” failed to force concessions. It fostered a more hardline stance in Tehran, which dramatically increased nuclear activity, heightening tensions with the west.

In theory, Trump’s latest campaign puts China — Iran’s largest trading partner and the only significant buyer of Iranian oil — in the US’s crosshairs. It also carries a warning for some of Washington’s allies, notably the United Arab Emirates and Turkey, which have served as hubs for Iranian businesses.
But Danny Citrinowicz, a former Iran analyst with Israeli military intelligence, said secondary sanctions were difficult to enforce.
He said the new campaign raised questions about Trump’s strategy as the administration has become locked in a battle of wills with the Islamic regime.

“They had the maximum pressure campaign before, so the question is what is the endgame for the administration?” Citrinowicz said. “They would have to create political friction with countries like China and Turkey — I’m not seeing them rushing to that.
“And the Iranians already know how to cope with secondary sanctions, building shell companies and things like that.”

Announcing the initiative on Monday, Bessent set no deadline for those trading with Iran to comply. He said Washington would give them time to “remedy bad behaviour”, while adding: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”

That appeared to be a tacit acknowledgment that the tactic risks reigniting a trade war with China, a month before Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping are due to meet in Washington. Beijing has warned the US it will “take all necessary measures” to protect itself from any expanded secondary sanctions.

China’s big state-owned refiners largely comply with sanctions on Iranian crude, but Beijing allows private sector refiners known as “teapots” to import and process Iranian oil. The US imposed sanctions on some of these refiners in May, but the Asian nation ordered domestic companies not to comply. Multiple China-linked entities have been sanctioned since 2018 over links to Iran.
China was Iran’s largest trading partner in the Iranian financial year to March, importing $11bn of goods, mainly crude and oil-related products, and exporting $13.4bn.
It was followed by the UAE, which had total trade with Iran of $21bn, while Nato member Turkey, which buys gas from the republic, had $13.5bn of trade, according to Iranian government data.
The UAE, a close US ally, said last week it was suspending “all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran . . . until further notice”.
It took the decision hours after accusing Iran of firing two ballistic missiles towards the Gulf state — and a day before Trump first declared “economic warfare”.

The UAE had taken a hawkish stance towards Tehran during the first months of the war after Iran fired almost 3,000 missiles and drones at the Gulf state. But Abu Dhabi had since sought to ease tensions through diplomacy and economic incentives.
This included allowing Iranian flights to Dubai to resume, the return of Iranians with UAE residency and traditional dhows to restart trade.
As a result, Iran had not fired directly at the UAE since mid-May. Travel agents in Tehran said this week that Iranian airlines were still flying to Dubai.

Turkey was also likely to take the threat of secondary sanctions seriously and would be wary of upsetting Trump, particularly as President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has sought to improve relations, said Galip Dalay, a senior research fellow at Chatham House.
“The political climate tells me that Turkey will be more careful given the stakes involved,” he said.
But he said Ankara would probably still allow trade in food and other non-sanctioned goods.
“Iran is a neighbouring state, there will be trade, it will never be reduced to zero,” Dalay said.
Sanctions and mismanagement have had a withering effect on Iran’s economy.

After Trump imposed his maximum-pressure policy, Iran’s economy contracted sharply for two years. Oil exports slumped, the rial plummeted and inflation soared. Iran has been cut off from global finance and has been battling a cost-of-living crisis since.

But apart from some specialist medicines, there were few shortages as the regime boosted domestic production and increased non oil-exports such as steel and petrochemicals.

Government entities and Iranian businessmen developed webs of trading routes to circumvent sanctions, using front companies and offshore offices in neighbouring states, including Turkey, Oman and the UAE.

Some Iranians bought properties worth $250,000 or more in Turkey to secure Turkish passports. Intermediaries traversed the region with suitcases packed with hundreds of thousands of dollars to keep the trade in goods flowing.
But now, after Iran has endured two wars in one year, the economy is in a far deeper malaise than in 2018.

The rial is hitting record lows against the dollar almost daily. Year-on-year inflation is soaring towards 90 per cent and several steel and petrochemical plants have been damaged or destroyed by war. The US is maintaining a naval blockade.
Iranian officials acknowledge the pain being heaped on the nation of about 90mn people.

Abdolnaser Hemmati, Iran’s central bank governor, this week said the economic situation over the past six months “has been very difficult”. Days earlier he had said Iran’s oil exports had reached “zero”.
But, he added, the “challenge is different from what the US is seeking”. He said the US “has done whatever it could to date and its latest measure will not make us collapse”.
He said Iran had been taking contingency measures such as depositing foreign currency “in various locations” to ensure Tehran had reserves to buy food and medicine, he said.

And Iran experts say any renewed economic pressure is highly unlikely to force Iran’s leadership to capitulate. Instead, it could harden its stance as it views the campaign as an attempt to foment social instability and push for regime change.
Recommended

“Iran did not collapse under Trump’s ‘maximum pressure’ policy and will not collapse this time,” said Saeed Laylaz, an Iranian analyst. “Iran is more experienced than it was in 2018; the world is more polarised than before and there are economies such as Iraq and Afghanistan that are dependent on Iran’s economy.”
The risk, analysts say, is that if US pressure intensifies Iran’s economic woes, that could trigger another military escalation.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top security official, this week warned the regime would regard “any country’s participation in or support for America’s economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war”.

Citrinowicz said: “If they [the regime] get to a decision where it’s capitulation or escalation, they will definitely choose escalation. If nothing moves, and Trump gets impatient, he will try to do other things to pressure Iran, like returning to some sort of kinetic action. We are seeing an impasse.”

Note to the prime minister: you won’t find the future in the past
articleContent: The writer is an FT contributing editor
British politics used to be about competing futures. It has turned into an argument about the past.

Newly installed as prime minister, Andy Burnham might have taken a cue from Labour predecessors such as Harold Wilson or Tony Blair. Wilson pledged to remake Britain in “the white heat of technology”. Blair promised “New Labour, New Britain”. Silly as they sound now, such slogans stirred the popular imagination.

Burnham’s instinct is to look backwards. He wants to recreate working-class, culturally conservative Labour, a party with its roots firmly in the north of England. The national mission is to overwrite the four decades of economic liberalism ushered in by Margaret Thatcher. The subtext is to wrest control of his party from metropolitan (southern) progressives to win back northern voters lost to Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform Party.

He is a follower rather than a leader of fashion in eulogising the past. Farage’s anti-migrant populists set the course. The Conservatives jumped on the bandwagon. The result is that Britain’s politics have become a fight about the two revolutions that shaped it during the second half of the 20th century.

The swinging sixties upended the cultural and social order. Alec Douglas-Home’s premiership sounded the last trumpet for the landed aristocracy’s grip on power. The strict social mores imposed, though rarely observed, by the ruling classes were heaped on a bonfire of inhibitions. Women and ethnic minorities took steps towards equality. Theatre censorship was abolished. The Rolling Stones filled the Albert Hall.

Twenty years later the hippies made way for yuppies when Thatcher’s economic liberalism blew up the postwar consensus. Nationalised industries were dismantled and the country’s industrial heartlands left to dereliction. The future belonged to the laissez-faire economics of the Washington consensus, open borders and the new financial capitalists.

There’s an element of caricature here. The settlements were never complete nor uncontested. The reactionary right railed against gender and ethnic equality, the left against the widening gulf between the winners and losers from globalisation. Strong economic growth, however, saw liberalism in both its guises, social and economic, absorbed into the political mainstream. For a time it seemed everyone, or almost everyone, could be a winner.

The 2008 global financial crash and the decade of austerity that followed gave the populists their opportunity. The future lost its shine. Voters concluded that their children would be even worse off. Why not reclaim the past?

Farage, a politician never troubled by consistency or coherence, promised to turn back the clock on both revolutions. The EU, immigrants, big business, progressives and establishment elites were easy scapegoats. The pitch is unabashed — foreigners would be banished, borders sealed and the country reclaimed for white working-class culture.

Snake oil though it is, no one should be surprised by its appeal in England’s left-behind provincial towns. Take away confidence in a better future and voters conclude they have nothing to lose. Those deserting Labour for the leftwing populism of the Green Party think the answer is a war on capitalism. Farage’s followers, skewed heavily towards older voters, blame immigrants.

Boris Johnson had his own fantasy. Outside the EU, the Tory author of Brexit declared, the nation could stand astride the world again as Global Britain. The present Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch mimics Reform by railing against diversity and inclusion. She would return Britain to an age when everyone agreed about the difference between men and women.

There is a political market for nostalgia, particularly among older voters. And the slump in Britain’s fortunes since 2008 has left a rich seam of grievance. But the past, as Burnham will discover, is a cul-de-sac. Myths about a better yesterday are not enough to build a governing majority.

Reform is certainly destabilising the mainstream parties, but has yet to show it can break the system. By following Farage rightward, Badenoch has secured her position among party activists at the cost of losing the support of moderate One Nation Tories. Much of shire England is being bequeathed to the centrist Liberal Democrats. Burnham will run into the same trap when middle-class professionals in the south turn their backs on cloth-cap Labour.
Nothing in politics is immutable and rules have exceptions, but elections in Britain are won by leaders who build a coalition behind an idea of a different future.

opinion content. 
The drip-drip US debt crisis
articleContent: Make no mistake, the US is suffering a debt crisis. It is, of course, not an acute emergency like Argentina’s multiple defaults this century or Greece’s woes in the 2010s, but it has the characteristics of a chronic disaster that everyone can see coming but the administration never does enough to avoid.

The most relevant measure of US federal government debt, that held by the public, has risen from $3.4tn in 2000 to $32.3tn now, or a rise from 33.7 per cent to more than 100 per cent of GDP in just over 25 years. More importantly, the burden of servicing that debt has doubled, from 11 per cent of tax revenues in 2000 to 21.5 per cent in the first 10 months of the current fiscal year. Because long-term borrowing costs are high, the US Treasury is increasingly financing the debt with short-term borrowing and the president is again pressuring the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates to make the numbers look better. This is the slippery slope of a slow-burn debt crisis.

With the US on a path to continue running deficits close to 6 per cent a year, even at full employment, the debt-to-GDP ratio is set to rise every year, increasing the call on tax revenues to service that debt and the pressure on the Fed to lower interest rates. The likelihood is not that this process ends in default or runaway inflation, but an ever-worsening problem for someone in future to solve. As I recently argued, rising deficits and debt-servicing costs no longer have the power to restore fiscal prudence.

Before examining solutions, it is worth asking why the US fiscal position has deteriorated so much this century. Since 2000, when the federal government ran a surplus of 2.3 per cent of national income, primary public spending (excluding net debt interest) has risen from 15.5 to 19.9 per cent of GDP. All of this increase can be accounted for by spending on services for an ageing population — social security, Medicare and veterans’ programmes.

On the tax side, revenues have fallen from 20 per cent to 17.2 per cent of GDP over the same period, partly a result of a cyclical peak in revenues at the end of the last millennium and partly the result of tax cuts. First came the Bush tax cuts, which were made permanent on a mostly bipartisan basis during the Obama administration, and then came the 2017 Trump tax cuts. The Centre for American Progress estimates that had the 1990s tax system remained intact, US public debt would be stable now, with a prospect of it declining in the decades ahead.

In the face of the fundamental long-term forces of rising age-related spending and unaffordable tax cuts, the inadequate recent response from the US administration has been a combination of bluster and panic.

Last week, Treasury secretary Scott Bessent promised again to focus on deficit reduction, but his talk has lost any credibility at this stage. Significant spending cuts were attempted by the now-disbanded Department of Government Efficiency and failed, while Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act spent the money raised by tariffs and no other tax increases are planned.

Where Bessent has taken steps to lower US government borrowing costs, such as proposing to swap a tiny slice of long-dated US debt with short-dated equivalents, they have been small, giving a sense of someone with few options. Having promised 3 per cent annual growth and a 3 per cent deficit, Bessent’s current record stands at roughly 2 per cent and almost 6 per cent respectively.

Faster growth would help with tax revenues, but would also probably increase interest rates, so the US has no sure-fire means of escaping its drip-drip debt crisis without significant spending cuts or tax increases. It does not need to eliminate the deficit, but does need to put debt back on a downward path, which almost certainly requires a balanced primary deficit — a metric that excludes net interest costs — something the US has not achieved since 2007 and not on a sustained basis since the 1990s.

Since cutting spending on pensions and healthcare for the elderly is difficult and undesirable, this and future US administrations should look at raising revenues in the least damaging way. The US has significantly cut tax rates for the richest this century, so some reversal of those would be likely and justified from a left-leaning president and Congress. But a valuable exercise in tax options and trade-offs, produced by the Tax Foundation, highlights the potential significant costs to growth and efficiency from narrow measures such as wealth taxes and tariffs. Its analysis suggests, not unreasonably, that broad-based rises in taxes on income or spending are best for raising large amounts of revenue to fund broad-based government programmes.

Other countries with similar difficulties would require different remedies. With its already high levels of taxation and healthy population that retires early, France needs first to encourage later retirement by cutting entitlements. The UK, which has already increased taxes sharply on those with high incomes, needs to ensure revenue raising is widely applied.

Meanwhile, financial markets are looking to the US for leadership, but it is absent. The instinct of this administration is to seek to talk its way out of its debt crisis rather than address the issues. While it denies there is a problem and tinkers around the edges, the drip-drip debt crisis will continue to build.
