/content/dcc9e095-92ca-40cf-98f7-33c07a2.title: FT Magazine. Fuchsia Dunlop’s mostly make-ahead Chinese feast
articleContent: When most people think of Chinese cooking, the images that spring to mind are hot dishes produced from a smoking wok or a billowing tower of steamers. But in many parts of China, meals typically begin with cold dishes that have been prepared in advance. In Sichuan, where I learnt to cook, the appetisers are often so scrumptious that they are the highlights of any menu. They whet the appetite for the hot dishes that will follow, and, for the home cook, remove much of the stress of entertaining.

Whenever I’m cooking for friends at home, I do my best to minimise the number of last-minute stir-fries on the menu so that I have time to talk to my guests and enjoy myself too. I usually make one or more Sichuanese cold dishes, with their excitingly layered flavours and characteristic edge of spice and tingliness. I’ll mix them up with recipes I’ve learnt in Shanghai and other parts of China, as well as some I’ve invented myself by blending Chinese and western culinary ideas.

A while ago, I noticed my guests relishing their first courses so much that I realised hot dishes could be optional, or could make up just a small part of the meal. (Sometimes people were just too full to cope with all the later dishes I had planned.) More recently, I’ve started creating whole menus of Chinese dishes served mezze-style, with bread on the side for mopping up delicious sauces (any bread is fine, but I particularly love to pick up heavenly Pakistani flatbreads from the Ararat bakery in Ridley Road Market in Dalston).

In summertime, such a meal is perfect for a table in the garden, though it can and should be enjoyed year round. On Boxing Day, Chinese cold dishes go beautifully with leftover Christmas meats, and you can serve them any time with a barbecue or a roast.

All the following cold dishes can easily be scaled up to cater for a big party, unlike stir-fries, and many can be prepared wholly or partly in advance. You can make larger portions of fewer dishes or the reverse: just to try to include a pleasing variety of colours and flavours. Lay the table with chopsticks or spoons and forks, as you please. Just don’t forget to supply bread to accompany the food.

The Chinese don’t normally require dessert, but often serve fruit at the end of a meal. At home in London, I like to offer what’s in season with bought sweetmeats for the western sweet tooth (Turkish delight, baklava, halva and/or chocolates are my personal standbys) and a pot of nice Chinese tea.
To serve six
Overnight fish-fragrant aubergines
Poached chicken with Sichuan pepper oil
Green beans with strange-flavour sauce
Sour-and-hot silken tofu with avocado
Lettuce salad with fermented tofu vinaigrette
Kohlrabi with spring onion oil
“Italian” wood ear mushroom salad
A day in advance
Make the fish-fragrant aubergines
Make the kohlrabi salad
Poach the chicken, allow to cool, then remove the meat from the bones and slice or shred
Mix up the strange-flavour sauce
Mix up the fermented tofu salad dressing
A day in advance or the morning of the party
Trim and boil the green beans
Rehydrate the wood ear mushrooms, then blanch and drain (keep immersed in cold water until needed)
At the last minute
Wash and spin the lettuce
Make the sauce for the chicken
Make the sauce for the tofu dish
Assemble all the dishes
To drink

With so many dishes on the table at once, choosing a specific wine can be challenging. It’s best to offer a few different bottles that guests can dip in and out of. Sparkling wine or a light and fresh white wine (avoiding anything too oaky) such as Riesling or Gewürztraminer work nicely, as does Pinot Noir or another light-bodied red.
Pantry essentials and cooking tools

Chinese food can be highly technical — there are numerous complicated cooking methods — but home cooking is often remarkably simple. You don’t need much kit; a good knife is essential, while a wok and a mandoline are useful to have too.
You do need half a dozen or so core seasonings such as Chinese vinegar and soy sauce, but once you have them in your cupboard, most recipes are at your fingertips.
Flowers and candles
A Chinese meal is typically served family-style, with everyone sharing the food that’s in the middle of the table, so flowers and candles usually get in the way — and can be high risk!
Liang ban yuxiang qiezi 凉拌鱼香茄子

I devised this version of my favourite Sichuanese dish to be served cool rather than hot in the traditional manner. It’s best made a day in advance to allow the aubergines to mingle with the flavours of the sauce.

Cut the aubergines into slices about 2cm thick and then chopstickable strips. Sprinkle with the salt, mix well and set aside for at least 30 minutes to drain out excess water. Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 200C/180C fan and line an oven tray with baking parchment.

Rinse the aubergines, drain well and pat dry with a clean tea towel or kitchen paper. Add 4 tbs of the cooking oil and mix well to coat the pieces evenly, then spread them out on the oven tray. Roast in the hot oven for about 30 minutes, until tender and golden. Then transfer to a container in which they can sit overnight in the fridge or larder.

Heat the remaining 2 tbs oil in a seasoned wok over a medium flame. Add the chilli bean paste or sambal oelek and sizzle gently until it smells delicious and the oil is red. Tip in the garlic and ginger, turn the heat up to high and stir-fry briefly until they smell wonderful too. Then pour in the hot water and add the sugar. Bring to the boil. Stir in the vinegar and 4 tbs of the spring onion greens and give them a brief lick of heat. Then pour the hot sauce over the aubergines. Turn the aubergines gently in the sauce, then leave overnight for the flavours to infuse. (If you eat it soon after cooking, the flavours won’t have had time to seep into the aubergines.)
Bring the aubergines to room temperature before serving. Garnish with the remaining spring onion greens.
Tengjiao liangban ji 藤椒凉拌鸡

This is my latest version of one of the great Sichuanese culinary ideas: the spicy cold chicken salad. In this case, it’s enlivened by the tingliness of Sichuan pepper oil. You can use leftover roast chicken (or turkey) for this recipe, but the meat will be most tender and silky if you poach the bird in the Chinese way. Bring to the boil enough water to fill a pan that will take the chicken without too much spare room. Immerse the bird in the boiling water, return to the boil and skim. For best results, then add a spring onion and a small piece of ginger, smacked to release their flavours. Turn the heat down to a gentle murmur and poach until the bird is just done; use a temperature probe to make sure the thickest part has reached 75C, or remove the chicken from the water and insert a skewer into the thickest part of the thigh to make sure the juices run clear. When the chicken is done, remove from the broth and allow to cool before deboning.
For the sauce
After the chicken is poached and deboned, cut the meat into chopstickable strips and pile up in a serving dish.

Then make the sauce. Combine all the ingredients except for the sesame seeds and spring onions in a small bowl and mix well. Before serving, pour this sauce over the chicken. Garnish with the sesame seeds and spring onions. Mix well before eating.
Guaiwei jiangdou 怪味豇豆

A classic Sichuanese strange-flavour sauce, named because it balances a whole gamut of seasonings, is so irresistible that it makes almost anything taste delicious. In Sichuan, people typically apply it to cold chicken or noodles, but I love to eat it with vegetables, as in the following recipe.
For the sauce

Place the sesame paste in a small bowl and stir and mash with a spoon until the consistency is even. Then gradually mix in the soy sauce and vinegar, taking care to incorporate completely so you end up with a smooth, emulsified sauce. Add the sugar and mix well. Stir in the Sichuan pepper (or Sichuan pepper oil), chilli oil and sesame oil.

Trim the beans and cut into bite-sized lengths. Tip into a panful of boiling water and boil for a few minutes until cooked to your liking (I prefer my beans just beyond the squeaky stage, at a point where they are tender but still a little taut). Then drain and cool immediately in a bowl of iced water or under the cold tap to preserve their bright green colour. Shake well in a colander and allow to dry off.
Tip the beans into a serving dish. Give the sauce another stir and then use it to dress the beans. Sprinkle over the sesame seeds.
Suanla niuyouguo doufu 酸辣牛油果豆腐

This dish showcases the surprisingly blissful harmony between the silky textures of tofu and avocado, with a classic Sichuanese dressing. Add the preserved duck egg (otherwise known as century egg) for an extra dimension of creaminess and umami flavour. The cured duck eggs (pidan 皮蛋), which can be found in most Chinese supermarkets, do not require cooking, but simply need to be shelled and rinsed before use.
For the dressing
Gently shell the preserved duck egg, if using, and rinse away any fragments of shell. Chop into small cubes. In a small bowl, mix together the vinegar, soy sauce and chilli oil to make the dressing.

To make it easier to extract the tofu from the packaging intact, turn the packet upside down, snip off the corners with a pair of scissors and then squeeze a bit to let some air in. Then remove the cover, drain off any excess water and tip the tofu on to a serving dish. Make one cut lengthwise down the block and then cut crossways into 0.5cm slices. Press gently on the tofu so that the slices lean to one side and then fan out on the dish.

Just before serving, scoop the avocado out of its shell and cut into small dice. Lay the avocado along the top of the tofu. Add the preserved egg, if using. Pour over the sauce, then sprinkle over the spring onion and sesame seeds and serve.
Furu selajiang ban shengcai 腐乳色拉酱拌生菜

This gorgeous vinaigrette, enriched with fermented tofu, is one I originally concocted as a dressing for steamed leeks, but it’s also fabulous with lettuce, sliced tomatoes and many other salad ingredients.
For the dressing

Place the tofu in a mixing bowl and mash with a spoon until smooth. Mix in the honey and mustard. Gradually whisk in the olive oil to make a smooth emulsion. Add the vinegar, and salt and pepper. Dilute with a little cold water if necessary to make a pourable consistency.
Wash and spin the lettuce leaves, then tear into pieces. Shortly before serving, dress and toss the salad. Finish with a sprinkling of sesame seeds.
Congyou pielan 葱油苤蓝
A classic Shanghainese flavouring technique, often used with chicken or slivered radish, applied here to kohlrabi.
Peel the kohlrabi. Cut into thin slices and then narrow slivers. Add the salt, massage it into the vegetable and set aside for at least 30 minutes to drain out excess water.
Squeeze out as much water as possible from the shredded vegetable. Stir in the sugar.

Heat the cooking oil in a wok until smoke rises from the sides and dipping a shred of kohlrabi or a scrap of spring onion into the oil produces a dramatic sizzle. Turn off the heat as you tip the spring onions into the hot oil and stir briskly as they release their fragrance. Add the kohlrabi and toss in the fragrant oil. You probably won’t need any more salt but taste to make sure. Set aside until needed.
Yidali liangban mu’er 意大利凉拌木耳
For fun one day, I decided to use Italian dressing ingredients with slippery-crisp wood ear mushrooms instead of Chinese rice vinegar and sesame oil. I’ve been making the dish ever since.

Cover the mushrooms generously with cold water and leave for an hour or so to rehydrate completely. When they are ready, tear larger pieces into suitably chopstickable pieces, discarding any knobbly bits. Bring a panful of water to the boil, add the mushrooms and blanch for a minute or so, then refresh in a colander under the cold tap and shake dry.
Add ¼ tsp salt, with more to taste, and then the other ingredients. Mix well and serve.
All recipes are from “Five Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchen”, Particular Books, published September 3. Pre-order via Waterstones

/content/fa2462dc-d3e6-4084-8d59-ad9bc63.title: Rob Armstrong’s guide to wearing colour
articleContent: Black, brown, navy blue, white, grey. A lot of well-dressed men stick to this austere palette. The main reason is versatility: you can mix those five colours together with minimal risk in any season and more or less anywhere. An additional appeal of the five-colour approach – for some men – is that it is unimpeachably masculine. Call that classicism or insecurity, as you like.

My view, however, is that nature wants more from us. Outside of homo sapiens, sexual dimorphism frequently cuts the other way. From mallards to mandrills, the males wear the paint. Both male and female fireflies light up, but it is the men who loop around, flashing their iridescence. The women wait, flashing back only if sufficiently impressed.
Yet a lot of our species can’t get past their caution. So here, for my shy brothers, is Armstrong’s Guide to Colour, organised by item and in ascending levels of difficulty.

Ties and pocket squares Too easy, really. Even an arch-traditionalist can handle a tie in yellow or pink, and be convinced to stick something bright in his jacket pocket on the weekend. This is an area where some restraint on colour can, ironically, work very well (though I do have a hot-pink knit tie that livens right up the standard blue suit).

Socks Here, things get a bit more interesting. There is a school of thought holding that the socks should be at least as dark as the trousers, because otherwise attention is drawn down. At this point in my life, however, I’m just as happy if people look at my feet. And a sock is one of the only places where strong reds look good (shorts is another). My favourite pair: apricot wool, over the calf.
Watch strap A leather or cloth watch strap in green, orange or red is fun. You can swap it out for a darker one for funerals and court appearances.

Shirts A nod to my father here: in all the years I knew him, I never saw him wear a solid colour shirt with a suit (and he was generally in a suit). He wore stripes and checks of all sorts, in all shades, and wasn’t afraid to combine them with a patterned tie. He looked great, so naturally I’ve rebelled and prefer solid blues and whites. Boring, I know, but they make it easier to lay on the colour elsewhere. I will say that I love a pale-yellow dress shirt though. Moving on to more casual stuff, the Hawaiian shirt is a cliché of the badly dressed man, but a slightly understated pattern can look superb; ask Magnum PI. I’m also currently on the hunt for the right Ankara (African wax print) shirt. Something turquoise-ish? Finally, the absolute classic: madras. No one looks bad in a madras shirt and khakis. Go for the gaudiest version you can find.

Trousers Loads of options here. There is a tradition among the Wasps of coastal New England of wearing trousers in bright pastels, sometimes embroidered with little whales or anchors in a contrasting shade. These are strangely appealing, but don’t try wearing them ironically. The only way to maintain your self-respect in lime-green trousers is by keeping a straight face and drinking a lot of gin and tonic. In winter-time, wide-wale corduroys in cheerful shades are a staple of British country-house style, but in a contemporary cut they look a lot less boring. Whatever the cloth, deep-yellow trousers work particularly well, for reasons that are unclear. My favourites are some mustard wide-leg numbers from Acne Studios.

Jackets are a great fortress of male colour conservatism. But the late style hero David Hockney showed how good a bright tweed jacket can look. A high-vis rain jacket is sunshine on a dreary day. And it is not written that a wool overcoat has to be grey, brown or camel-coloured. Gloverall makes duffel coats in rust and loden green.

Suits Master-level stuff. You have to really consider how much wear you will get out of a very bright coloured suit. But I have one in a dark-green flannel I wear all the time. Something in burnt-orange Donegal tweed maybe?
Conclusion The world can be a pretty drab place. More men should rebel.

articleContent: The price of liquefied natural gas in north-west Europe surged to its highest level in more than three years, as the continent braces for tight winter supply as a result of the Middle East conflict.

Buyers were paying $22.83 for 1mn British thermal units at the start of this week, more than double the price a year ago and the highest since January 2023, according to Argus Media. Prices on Tuesday dipped marginally to $22.23.
Disruption to flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which ordinarily handles around a fifth of the world’s LNG supplies, has sent prices surging since the start of the Iran war earlier this year.

Gas markets have been affected even more than oil, which has also risen this year, because shipping crude is simpler and does not require such complex and expensive vessels. Some crude shipments have left the Gulf in recent months, albeit far below prewar levels.
In contrast, only eight LNG carriers exited the strait in July, according to data compiled by Kpler, compared with around three per day before the war.

Shipments could be curtailed further after Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority threatened dozens of ships with fines or confiscation on Sunday. The list of 46 blacklisted vessels included 10 LNG carriers.
Gas traders are losing confidence that shipments through the narrow waterway will restart soon, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus.

While all LNG importers have been hit by the reduced flows out of the Middle East, Europe was in a particularly vulnerable position as gas inventories were at lower levels than usual before the war began.
In the first few months of the conflict, Europe managed its needs by reducing the amount of gas it injected into storage, but this has meant its facilities have restocked at a slower pace than usual.
Net injections in Europe averaged 3 terawatt hours per day in August, down from 3.6 TWh a year ago, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data.

Analysts have warned for several months that gas storage levels are too low. Meanwhile, gas futures prices for the coming months have stayed broadly flat, giving traders little incentive to stock up now and then sell later in the winter when demand is higher.
Under more normal circumstances, traders buy gas during the low-demand season, pay to store it and then sell it for a profit in the winter.

As a result, European buyers are now competing with Asia for supplies, pushing up prices there too. Platts JKM, the Asian LNG benchmark, gained 13 per cent in August, hitting $24.08 per MMBtu on Tuesday, just shy of its wartime peak of $25.41.

Gas traders are closely watching European policymakers for any sign that they may intervene in the market. German storage is 50 per cent full and the law obliges the government to buy and store gas if private companies do not use their booked storage capacity.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
In the meantime, analysts warn prices may rise further.

Asian buyers reduced their imports early in the conflict, helping to tamp down global prices, but benchmark European gas prices would need to rise above €100 a megawatt hour to “more significantly discourage Asian LNG demand”, said Goldman Sachs in a note on Sunday. Contracts were trading at around €66 per MWh on Tuesday.

China, Asia’s biggest LNG importer, has demonstrated less willingness to compete with Europe for cargoes in response to tight global supplies this year than it did in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

However, the region’s other buyers are showing more willingness to pay higher prices than in the past. There has been “sustained demand above $20 per MMBtu from typically price-sensitive countries in South and South-East Asia”, said Argus’ Senior.

/content/35a82994-31cf-4aaa-b0ee-03002a5.title: Private equity growth funds attract record first-half inflows as sector rebounds
articleContent: US private equity funds that invest in fast-growing companies without taking a controlling stake raised a record amount of capital in the first half of this year, in a sign of their strong recovery from a 2023 fundraising slump.

Growth funds attracted $33.2bn in the first six months of this year, the highest first-half total on record and a 36 per cent jump from a year earlier, according to data from Preqin. Fundraising across other private equity strategies grew 20 per cent over the same period.
The surge comes even as the number of growth funds raising capital dipped to 87 in the first half from 96 a year earlier.

Large, established managers and smaller specialist funds are among the beneficiaries of the inflows, helped by surging interest in AI-related companies and valuations that in some cases are still below the highs hit in the industry’s 2021 boom during the coronavirus pandemic.
“I think the recovery is definitely real,” said Jeff Machlin, managing partner of Connecticut-based Wingman Growth Partners, which closed a $215mn growth fund in June, “but it’s selective in nature”.

Fundraising for US private equity growth funds peaked in 2021, when $67bn was raised for the year, as monetary and fiscal stimulus during the pandemic helped drive a technology investment rush that pushed valuations sharply higher and often prioritised revenue growth over profitability.

But as doubts grew over whether rapidly expanding companies could ultimately deliver the profits implied by their valuations, investors raced to pull back from growth equity, with fundraising tumbling to just $29bn in 2023.

“The whole asset class got penalised,” said Hugh MacArthur, chair of Bain & Company’s global private equity practice. “Investors basically said: ‘Stop — I don’t know what anybody’s doing, so I’m not investing.’”

A drop-off in initial public offerings and dealmaking meant there were fewer exits available for private investments, which limited the payouts back to investors and reduced their ability to put money to work again in new funds.

However, growth equity fundraising has risen in both of the past two years and is on track to grow again this year. A survey by consultancy McKinsey & Co of 296 institutional investors in January found 46 per cent of respondents planned to increase their allocation to growth private equity in the coming three years. That compared with 35 per cent for buyout funds and 41 per cent for venture capital.

Private company valuations had “come down pretty materially” compared with 2021, said Chris Cavanagh, general partner at Boston-based Guidepost Growth Equity, which raised $521mn for its latest fund in January, adding that investors could now “enter at more attractive multiples”.

The huge success of AI start-ups has also helped make growth equity more attractive, say investors, as pension plans and endowments seek exposure to what they think could be the next technology winner.

“There is more demand from allocators to make sure that they have access within their portfolios to the next OpenAI, Anthropic or SpaceX, to ensure that they’re not kind of missing the boat,” said Luke Riela, who advises institutional investors on private market investments at consultancy Meketa.

However, investors have also been selective in the funds they back, with much of the money flowing into a handful of big funds, which are often more able to absorb large inflows from institutional investors. Three growth funds — including the $10bn Thrive X fund, run by Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital — accounted for more than half of the capital raised in the first six months of this year.

“This is not where the best returns are,” said an executive at a state pension plan that had invested in large growth funds this year, speaking about large funds in general. “This is ‘I think I can safely put $500mn to work.’”

Smaller, specialised growth funds have also found success. Sheldon Lewis, managing partner at San Diego-based Blueprint Equity, said he was able to raise $333mn for a fund focused on early-stage AI-driven software companies, helped by strong returns from its previous funds.
“When you come back to your investors to raise your next fund and you’ve already paid them quite a lot of money, they are obviously a lot more inclined to give you money down,” said Lewis.

Despite the momentum, many growth funds are still struggling to raise capital as exits remain challenging and traditional software, once a major focus for growth equity investment, faces the threat posed by rapid developments in AI.

Sarah Sandstrom, head of North America private equity placement at Campbell Lutyens, a financial advisory, said growth funds launched in 2022 had so far returned virtually no cash to investors, while those launched in 2021 had returned about 60 cents for every dollar invested — low levels by industry standards.
“The last wave of growth investing has yet to really give people confidence that it’s bearing fruit by and large,” she said.
Bruce MacDonald, chief investment officer of the $2.5bn Virginia Commonwealth University Investment Management Company, said he has stayed away from traditional growth funds.
They are “so dependent on software, which is a very risky place to be investing”, he said.

/content/acb64e29-a3ce-4282-82b0-6b7b5dd.title: US grain farmers pummelled as Iran war triggers surge in costs
articleContent: Farmers in America’s Corn Belt say they are facing their worst crisis in 40 years, as an explosion in diesel and fertiliser costs triggered by Donald Trump’s Iran war pushes grain producers to the brink.

The growing strains are the latest sign of how the conflict in the Middle East, now in its sixth month, is reverberating through the US’s heartland ahead of crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

“Inputs are way out of whack,” said Matt Bailey, who grows corn and soyabeans in eastern Nebraska. He said 11-52-0, a phosphorus-rich fertiliser used at planting time that was priced at $470 a tonne 10 years ago, now costs more than $900. “Where do you start with that? How do you budget for that?”

The huge uptick in prices for fuel and crop nutrients since the US launched its attack on Iran in February came with American farmers already struggling after years of low grain prices and falling incomes.
Many also see themselves as casualties of Trump’s trade wars, which they say have hurt US agricultural exports, particularly soyabean sales to China.
“This is the worst financial downturn in the sector since the 1980s,” said John Hansen, president of Nebraska Farmers Union.

A recent study by the American Farm Bureau Federation, an industry group, found that, without government assistance, farmers growing nine principal crops — including corn — will lose $31bn this year and $32bn in 2027.

Faith Parum, an economist with the AFBF, said losses for corn producers would stand at $131 per acre this year, rising to $167 in 2027. For soyabeans, the figure is $80 per acre in losses this year and $138 next year. She said 2027 would mark the sixth year of negative returns for most major row crops in the US.

The struggles for Midwestern farmers show how concerns over affordability, the inflationary impact of the Iran war and the adverse effects of Trump’s tariffs are reaching greater segments of the US population — from working-class families in big cities to rural communities in the heartlands.

A recent FT poll found that more than 53 per cent of registered voters said their finances had deteriorated since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, a result that could spell trouble for Republican hopes of retaining control of Congress.

“We’ve got 71 days [until the midterm elections] and right now we don’t have a positive message to sell farm country, and we haven’t since ‘liberation day’ last year,” the Republican senator Thom Tillis said on Monday.
Recommended

Trump has vowed to support farmers, saying in June that “we’re never going to let you down”. In the same month his administration requested an $11bn funding package for farmers that would provide emergency assistance to row crop and speciality crop producers. But farming groups say it is not enough.

Some of his attempts to tackle rising food prices have triggered a backlash from the agricultural sector. Last week Trump enraged cattle farmers by announcing a 90-day waiver of tariffs on up to 300,000 tonnes of beef imports, a move some ranchers called a “betrayal”.

But many farmers say it is Trump’s war in Iran that has had the most sweeping effect on their businesses. The sharp slowdown in traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up the price of diesel and disrupted the global supply of fertiliser, which had already surged in 2022 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“The [Iran] war has made so much uncertainty for us as farmers,” said Pam Johnson, who farms in northern Iowa and is a former president of the National Corn Growers Association. “It’s projected that farmers aren’t going to make any money for the next two years.”

The average cost for diesel — widely used to power agricultural equipment — has shot up to $5.45 a gallon nationwide, compared with $3.81 before the war, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Interest payments, labour costs and the price of farm machinery had also increased, said Brad Lubben, a professor of agricultural economics at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln.
“If you look at all the components of the production budget, most of them have gone up substantially over the past few years,” he said.
Drought and hot, dry conditions across the US corn belt have compounded some farmers’ woes.
John Dittrich, who grows corn and soyabeans near Meadow Grove, Nebraska, said extreme weather was a growing problem.
“Our droughts are worse, our heavy rainfall events are worse, our winds are worse.”
Dittrich said the risk to his business from weather events and rising costs was “higher than it’s ever been in my 44-year career”.

“Our costs of production are very high and then the instability and the unknowns of every variable that affects both our production and the prices we receive for our commodities are just unprecedented.”

The weather is helping to push up corn prices, as traders pare back expectations for the 2026 harvest. US corn for delivery in December has already jumped 10 per cent this month to $5.15 a bushel, the highest level since 2023.

With the price of other commodities such as soyabeans and wheat also rallying in recent days, experts fear that this could push up inflation, already running above the Federal Reserve’s 2 per cent target.

“This will definitely mean higher food prices,” said Brian Choi, chief executive of the Food Institute, a research organisation. With corn prices rising almost 20 per cent this year, “it will eventually make its way to the consumer”.

Nebraska is among the states hit hardest by the drought. From January to July, it received 11.86 inches of precipitation — about 3.1 inches below normal. That made it the 18th-driest January-July period since records began in 1895.
Recommended

“I’ve got some good friends on the Sandhills [a vast area of north-central and western Nebraska] that haven’t hardly gotten any rain since last fall,” said Del Ficke, a cattle farmer in Pleasant Dale, Nebraska.

Recent rainfall provided some relief but came too late for many farmers. “A lot of damage [to the crop] has already been done,” said Hansen of the Nebraska Farmers Union. “It’s like closing the stable door after the horse has bolted.”

Bailey said the poor weather would probably affect his yields this year. “Because of all the early-season stress that happened, I don’t see it being a bin-buster, by any means,” he said. “Especially if you factor in all the dry land . . . that just didn’t get the water and got beat to crap for six weeks.”

/content/d18b330f-1cc2-4f83-9720-5ab5b13.title: JPMorgan relaxes restrictions on borrowing against SpaceX shares
articleContent: JPMorgan Chase is relaxing its approach to lending money against shares held by employees and early investors in companies that have recently gone public, as the US bank seeks to win clients from emerging tech giants.

JPMorgan’s typical policy is not to accept as collateral shares in a company that has been listed for fewer than 135 days. However, it told bankers ahead of SpaceX’s blockbuster initial public offering in June that it would lend against shares in Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company sooner, according to people familiar with the matter.

Bankers inside JPMorgan expect the lender to have a similar approach when Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, goes public, though no final decision has been made. JPMorgan earned $75mn from its role on the SpaceX listing.
JPMorgan’s move underscores the efforts asset managers are making to win business from the huge wealth being generated by the AI boom.
Its policy was already longer than the 30 days that broker-dealers generally wait to lend against shares when they worked on the IPO under US securities rules.
Other banks such as Goldman Sachs will typically not wait longer than the 30-day period before engaging in this type of lending, said people familiar with the matter. Goldman declined to comment.

JPMorgan said the bank’s policy remains unchanged. “Our practices exceed regulatory requirements, and we have always assessed transactions on a case-by-case, client-by-client basis, factoring in elements such as market liquidity,” it said.
Anthropic declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
Top engineers at AI labs can earn millions and sometimes tens of millions of dollars, part of which is company stock.

In the second quarter, Morgan Stanley’s wealth management business took in more than $74bn in net new assets from IPOs, including SpaceX, through its work managing employee equity plans for companies. The bank has said this performance was “not a one-time hit” with a pipeline of future big stock market listings.

Some Anthropic employees are sitting on tens of millions of dollars. Anthropic was valued at $18bn in 2024, and was most recently valued at $965bn. The company said in June it had confidentially filed for an IPO and investors expect the AI start-up to float at a valuation of $2tn or more in October.
Borrowing against shares can be a more popular option than selling for wealthy individuals, to minimise tax impacts.

A crucial question for banks examining collateral quality is how easily it can be liquidated, and private shares are less easily tradeable than public stock. Even after a company has gone public, there can also be lock-up agreements that place restrictions on stock sales. Shares after an IPO can also be more volatile.
Nevertheless, the glut of highly valued tech companies going public represents an enormous opportunity for Wall Street groups looking to manage money for the newly wealthy.

Other wealth management firms have also been working to entice the employees of big AI groups before they go public, cutting fees and hiring staff around Silicon Valley in an attempt to win over workers at OpenAI and Anthropic before their IPOs turn out a new class of millionaires.
Additional reporting by Harriet Clarfelt

/content/a40460fa-88fa-437f-99c6-828b263.title: The old asbestos town at the heart of the rare earths race
articleContent: For decades the remote town of Minaçu thrived off its asbestos mine, the last in the Americas, before the one-time miracle material’s links to deadly diseases led to bans and an industry decline.

Today, the municipality deep in Brazil’s interior is at the centre of a global race for the rare earth minerals essential to electronics, clean energy and defence tech, which have become a flashpoint in the US-China trade war.

In a wilderness of green peaks and valleys, a mining group claims to have the only site outside Asia digging up some of the scarcest types of these metals at scale, with financial backing from Washington.

Residents believe it can revive the fortunes of this community of 27,000 in the tropical savannah state of Goiás. Since commercial rare earths production in the South American country began here a couple of years ago, newcomers were arriving again, said Minaçu’s mayor Carlos Alberto Leréia.
“It’s a tremendous gain. The place was on its way to becoming a ghost town,” he added. “It’s as if you’re drowning and then a rope appears — you have to grab hold of it.”

The sentiment echoes wider optimism about Brazil’s potential to be a major player in a strategically important sector. Though its output remains modest for now, the country possesses the second-largest rare earth reserves after China, according to the US Geological Survey.
A group of 17 metallic elements required in small quantities for many high-tech applications, rare earths are relatively abundant in the planet’s crust but difficult to extract and separate.

With control over much of the world’s rare earth mining and a virtual monopoly on their processing, Beijing restricted exports last year in retaliation against President Donald Trump’s tariffs, intensifying a hunt for new sources.

That search has brought the Americans to Minaçu, where the mine’s owner Serra Verde is scaling up. “The objective is to be an alternative in the west for the production of rare earths,” said sustainability director Pedro Burnier at the company’s complex, which has received more than a billion dollars in investment.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
USA Rare Earth, in which Washington owns a minority stake, announced a $2.8bn takeover of Switzerland-based Serra Verde in April.

“The rest of the world will [now] have access to the heavy rare earths that, quite frankly, we are all too dependent on China for today,” USA Rare Earth’s outgoing chief executive, Barbara Humpton, told the FT.
The project has also secured more than $500mn in loans from the US International Development Finance Corporation, a public lender.

The mine has become a linchpin of US efforts to break free of Chinese dominance over the minerals, thanks to the presence of two of the most critical heavy rare earths, so-called because of their higher atomic weight. Dysprosium and terbium are found in powerful magnets for guided missiles, electric vehicle motors and wind turbines, helping maintain magnetic strength at high temperatures.
“They are today the most highly valued,” said Burnier.

By next year, Serra Verde aims to account for more than half the heavy rare earth elements supply outside China. Yet its production target of 6,400 tonnes of total rare earth oxides still represents just a fraction of the overall 390,000 tonnes mined globally in 2025, according to USGS figures.

During construction, the company signed long-term supply deals with buyers in China, reflecting the lack of rare earth processing elsewhere, but later slashed their contract periods. Instead, Serra Verde now has a 15-year agreement to sell its output to an entity backed by the US government and private capital. This will then allocate stocks to processors, with guaranteed minimum prices in case China floods the market.
“Costs here are higher than in China, possibly due to our greater focus on environmental concerns,” said Fernando Landgraf, professor of metallurgical engineering at the University of São Paulo.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

American officials have long eyed Brazil’s critical minerals. However, as US-Brazil diplomatic relations have plunged over trade and political disputes, the Serra Verde offtake arrangement weakens Brasília’s negotiating power with Washington, according to Rob Muggah, co-founder of think-tank Igarapé Institute in Rio de Janeiro.
“The most serious concern is that the agreement could deprive Brazil of the feedstock needed to build its own rare earth industry,” added Muggah.

Ahead of a re-election bid in October, leftwing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has framed the resources as a matter of national sovereignty and wants his country to develop value-added manufacturing around the minerals rather than just export raw materials. His main opponent, rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, has pledged closer co-operation with the US on the metals.
Serra Verde said it already undertook significant processing in Minaçu, turning the clays into an intermediate substance containing light and heavy rare earths.
However, the next industrial step — separating the elements into high-purity individual oxides — is more difficult. New refineries are planned by companies in Europe, North America and Australia.

With scant arable land and limited industry around Minaçu, locals hope rare earths will help the area move on. The legacy of asbestos is visible from artificial terraced hills of mining waste that loom over the town’s streets.
Founded in the 1960s, the mine has stopped and restarted since Brazil’s Supreme Court banned asbestos use in 2017, but its closure is widely considered inevitable.

Thais Oliveira, an ice cream parlour owner, remembers hearing dynamite blasts and her mother’s stories of cleaning the dust that snowed down. Her sales are up about a quarter since Serra Verde started operations.

“The town was dead and there was nobody on the streets. Now it’s going back to what it was before,” said the 33-year-old mother.
However, not everyone is happy. Several residents said streams near Serra Verde had on occasion become discoloured with an oily residue after heavy downpours since the mine opened.
Smallholder Aníbal de Oliveira, 77, said: “The run-off is dirty. The water turns reddish because the soil is red up there.”

Serra Verde said it took “seriously any potential environmental impacts” and worked closely with regulators to identify and mitigate issues. It received a fine after self-reporting unlicensed deforestation in 2023.

The miner has 600 direct employees and hundreds of contractors, but some inhabitants wonder how far the benefits will spread. Hotel receptionist Nathanael Pereira Rodrigues took a course to train as a truck driver in anticipation of a vacancy but is yet to be called.
“They only want skilled labour, with two or three years of experience,” said the 23-year-old soon-to-be father. “It’s frustrating, but I’m not going to give up.”

For all the hype around Brazil’s rare earths, Serra Verde’s long journey — roughly 15 years from first survey to shipment — shows the bureaucratic and financial hurdles that face such projects. Others are under development, though entrepreneurs often lament scarce funding and environmental permitting times.

Even so, mayor Leréia remains bullish: “Brazil is going to become a top player in rare earths.”

Additional reporting by Camilla Hodgson and Beatriz Langella. Data visualisation by Andrew Francisco and cartography by Chira Fae Llarena

/content/e08d7f0e-f9fb-45a4-a1ef-025a75a.title: Iranians queue for petrol as US blockade bites
articleContent: Long queues have formed at petrol stations around Tehran as the US blockade triggers fuel shortages and spreads alarm among motorists in a sign of the war’s growing strain on the Iranian economy.

The rush comes as Donald Trump’s administration outlined a new campaign of what it called “economic warfare” against Tehran, which the Energy Optimisation Organisation — an Iranian state body tasked with managing fuel resources — warned was facing a “critical” shortfall of petrol.

One petrol station attendant in the capital reported that people were rushing to fill up “even before their tanks are empty because they worry that the war might start over again or that prices will rise”. A limit of 20 litres per car meant that motorists had to keep returning, said the attendant, who did not want to be named.

The country, a major crude exporter, has long relied on petrol imports to make up the shortfall in its supplies. But the US naval blockade — in place since July 14 — has severely curtailed Iran’s ability to secure fuel, while the US and Israeli bombing campaign destroyed some of its refining capacity in the early weeks of the war, which began in February.
The EOO said Iran was currently 15mn litres short of its total daily petrol demand of 135mn.

US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent on Monday said Washington was expanding the scope of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners as it sought to tighten the economic and financial noose on Tehran.
The regime insists the nation is able to resist US pressure and has refused to agree to Trump’s demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Both sides accuse each other of violating a June deal designed to gradually reopen the critical waterway and lay the foundation for talks over a final settlement, and Iran’s leaders argue that Tehran must inflict a greater cost on Washington before agreeing to end the war.
Imports from northern routes have also become severely constrained because of the effects of the Ukraine war and Russian losses of a significant portion of its refining capacity.

Iranian officials say the fuel shortage has been exacerbated by a subsidy system that provides the country’s 90mn population with some of the world’s cheapest petrol, with motorists charged between IR15,000 ($0.0075) and IR50,000 per litre.

The government, which has spent months tapping into Iran’s strategic reserves, says the current pricing and quota mechanism is no longer sustainable because of soaring inflation and the supply disruptions caused by the war.

President Masoud Pezeshkian this month said selling petrol at below-market prices placed immense pressure on government resources required for food subsidies and support for workers. “Who said the government should buy petrol at 1.3mn rials per litre and then sell it for 15,000 rials?” he said.
And Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei, the head of Pezeshkian’s office, on Monday said the government intended to reduce quotas but that a final decision on pricing had not been made.

“There are uncertainties regarding the social, economic and security implications of any pricing policy,” he said, adding that while the government would definitely reduce quotas, “people may have to pay higher prices for consumption beyond their allocated quotas”.
But the prospect of raising fuel prices for a population whose purchasing power is weaker than ever is deeply sensitive.
Iran’s national currency has plunged to a new low of IR2mn to the dollar in recent days, with year-on-year inflation at nearly 90 per cent and food inflation at about 130 per cent.
Recommended

A pilot project to increase petrol prices in Kerman province this month was halted just a few hours after its implementation. Suggestions of price rises recall memories of 2019, when an overnight increase triggered deadly protests across Iranian cities.
Petrol prices were a kind of “barometer of inflation” and liable to cause a very severe shock to the economy, said Morteza Behrouzifar, an energy analyst based in Tehran.
Behrouzifar suggested the government continue short-term supply measures while trying to improve public transport, the domestic automotive industry and the refining industry.

“People are already under tremendous pressure,” he said. “If the government now wants to address this issue through an increase in petrol prices, it could have undesirable social and economic consequences.”

/content/940339db-b5b5-4b53-95e6-cfbc42e.title: NatWest plots push into US market
articleContent: NatWest is making a fresh push into the US market more than a decade after the financial crisis forced it into retreat, taking advantage of loosening rules on UK banks’ overseas operations.

The high-street bank secured approval from the US Federal Reserve last Thursday to set up a representative office in Connecticut that would “act as a liaison with current and prospective US customers of the bank”.
NatWest currently has a US-licensed broker-dealer based in Stamford, Connecticut, that can execute trades for institutional clients such as hedge funds.
But the new representative office will allow the bank to step up its marketing of products to US clients and cultivate relationships with American companies.

It marks the first significant attempt by NatWest to crack the US market since the financial crisis and follows a change to ringfencing rules by previous chancellor Rachel Reeves to help make UK banks more competitive.
These changes in January 2025 were a key factor in NatWest’s US push, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Rules introduced after the 2008 crisis mandated banks to separate their retail operations from their riskier investment-banking activities.

They also prohibited ringfenced banks from establishing branches or subsidiaries outside the European Economic Area to insulate them from risks tied to overseas operations. That was reversed as part of a deregulatory push by Reeves to unlock capital for banks.

NatWest has been pursuing a more aggressive growth strategy since its return to private ownership last year, when the UK government finally divested its stake in the lender acquired as part of a £45.5bn bailout. It completed the £2.7bn takeover of wealth manager Evelyn Partners this year as part of an effort to diversify its sources of income.
Higher interest rates have buoyed the profits of UK banks, with the big four of Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and HSBC reporting £29bn in pre-tax profits in the first half of the year.
This has allowed NatWest and Lloyds to reconsider international expansion in earnest for the first time since the financial crisis.

In its strategic update announced in July, Lloyds Banking Group announced its intentions to grow its North American business to 30 per cent of revenues for its corporate and institutional bank by 2030.
RBS, as NatWest was formerly known, entered the US market in 1988 through its purchase of Citizens Financial Group, which it used as a vehicle to complete a string of acquisitions.

However, RBS’s near-collapse during the financial crisis forced the lender to sell off its international empire, and it completed its exit from Citizens in 2015. Around the same time, it sold a portfolio of US loans belonging to its corporate bank to the Japanese lender Mizuho.

Since then it has retained a small presence in the US aimed at serving British clients with operations there. The bank makes the bulk of its revenue in the UK but it also has a branch in Germany and non-bank subsidiaries with offices in India, Finland, Sweden and Switzerland.

/content/1b1c357f-6a1c-4ce3-bb47-980c3de.title: China challenges Korean champions in flash memory race
articleContent: YMTC aims to overtake Samsung and SK Hynix to become the world’s largest Nand flash memory producer as the Chinese company gears up for a stock market listing.

The Wuhan-based group told investors and stakeholders in recent IPO preparation meetings that it wants to take the global Nand crown by as soon as the end of 2027, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Last week, YMTC filed for an IPO to raise Rmb33bn ($5bn), mostly to upgrade production facilities as well as for research and development, according to a prospectus published on the Shanghai Stock Exchange website.
The chipmaker had operating revenue of Rmb47bn ($7bn) in the first quarter. Net profit was Rmb33bn — more than double the total for the whole of 2025, according to its IPO prospectus.

YMTC, which is yet to set a timeline for its market debut, is expected to reach a market valuation above Rmb1tn ($150bn) after trading begins, making it the second-largest IPO in China this year. However, the shares will probably be priced conservatively under regulatory guidance, according to a banker involved in the process.
Market consensus put its IPO valuation at Rmb200bn to Rmb300bn, while the exact figure was yet to be finalised during the listing process, they added.
YMTC has accelerated its IPO plans following the successful debut of CXMT, another Chinese leading memory-chip maker that primarily makes DRam chips.
Its valuation surged more than 400 per cent late last month after raising $9bn in Asia’s largest IPO this year. CXMT is now China’s most valuable listed company, worth $580bn.

Nand chips are a type of hardware that can store data without a power source and are most commonly found in devices such as smartphones and tablets. DRam chips store data temporarily and can be used in computers as well as for AI processing tasks.

Unlike GPUs, which require leading-edge lithographic production equipment that US sanctions actively target, memory manufacturing relies heavily on stacking architecture and process optimisation — areas where Chinese firms have rapidly narrowed the capability gap.
By leveraging state subsidies and a world-leading electronics supply chain, YMTC and CXMT are both capturing a bigger slice of the Nand and DRam markets.

The gains provide them with both the cash flow needed to fund further research and the leverage to establish China as an indispensable player in the global technology ecosystem, regardless of western trade barriers.
According to TrendForce, a research and consulting company, YMTC ranked third globally and first in China among global Nand producers in the first quarter, behind Samsung and SK Hynix.

The global Nand market size was estimated to be worth $71bn last year, a figure expected to surge to more than $300bn in 2026, according to TrendForce. The market is expected to be worth about $490bn by 2030.

Many investors are concerned that CXMT and YMTC’s ambitious expansion plans will cause memory chip prices to slide, ending a bull run for stocks in the sector. They have been among the biggest winners from the AI frenzy.
Recommended

Joanna Yang, a portfolio manager at Ninety One, said: “For global investors, one question is how these Chinese companies’ capacity expansion is going to impact the supply-demand dynamics for memory. This is a global product — it has global pricing.”
Cameron Chui, Asia equity strategist at JPMorgan Private Bank, said: “Is China adding new capacity? Absolutely.”

However, he remained optimistic on the sector due to rising demand for memory chips needed for training AI models. “Supply is growing but we think demand grows faster. We think it’s not enough to balance the market.”
YMTC did not respond to a request for comment.

/content/0c59f1d7-2197-406b-ba9b-6592c12.title: SpaceX commits $100bn to Louisiana space base
articleContent: SpaceX has confirmed plans to build a $100bn launch site in Louisiana for its Starship rocket as Elon Musk’s company plans to expand its operations to support its vision of orbital data centres and flights to the Moon and Mars.

The project was unveiled by Louisiana’s Republican governor Jeff Landry at an event on Tuesday alongside SpaceX’s president Gwynne Shotwell. The facility will span roughly 125,000 acres in an area known as Pecan Island on the Gulf Coast roughly three hours west of New Orleans.
SpaceX intends to start construction next year and fly its first rockets from the base in 2029.
“This will be a project like no other. Another piece of science fiction transported into reality or what I call science fact,” Shotwell said.

SpaceX is seeking to rapidly increase the pace of rocket launches after raising $86bn in the largest initial public offering in June. The company has set out ambitious targets including reaching Mars using reusable rockets, putting data centres into orbit and developing advanced AI models.

The company’s 407-foot-tall Starship rocket is central to the group’s ambitions. SpaceX plans to reuse both stages of the rocket while dramatically increasing the payload it can carry, enabling it to launch more equipment into orbit including larger satellites. Efforts to refuel the spacecraft while in orbit are central to delivering lunar and Martian missions.
Starship has flown 13 times but has experienced a number of technical setbacks with SpaceX racing to deliver an operational rocket.

The company has expanded its presence in Texas, home of its current launch site. Local residents in the area around the base near Boca Chica Beach voted to incorporate last year under the name Starbase, Texas.
Musk moved the legal base of his companies Tesla and SpaceX to Texas after clashing with state courts in Delaware over his pay and other issues.

Louisiana’s development agency said it had offered SpaceX a “competitive incentives package” to win the project and that in lieu of local taxes the company has agreed to pay $25mn annually to the local parish.
Some residents around the proposed Louisiana site have opposed SpaceX’s project since the company sketched out its plans earlier this year because of environmental concerns.

ExxonMobil gave up the Pecan Island site following a legal settlement stemming from allegations that its activities were worsening pollution in the area. The oil major said in court filings that it considered the proceedings meritless. The Guardian previously reported these developments.

Landry on Tuesday said: “These acres will be home to SpaceX and it will be built by Louisiana hands on Louisiana soil . . . This will be the place which America reaches farther than it has ever reached before.”

SpaceX’s planned site will include five launch complexes with two launch pads at each facility. The company will also build residential housing for employees and their families similar to its Starbase hub in Texas.

/content/21ef2743-2cc2-41ef-8329-84adce6.title: Waymo picks Munich for first EU robotaxi launch
articleContent: Waymo is planning to launch its robotaxis in Munich next year, the US tech company’s first market in the EU, as Germany tries to bolster its struggling automotive sector.

The Alphabet-owned company announced on Tuesday that it aims to start commercial ride-hailing services in the German city towards the end of 2027 as it steps up its international push. It is already testing in Tokyo and London.
“Munich is a world-class hub for mobility and engineering, and becoming part of this city marks an important milestone in our global expansion,” said Waymo’s co-chief executive Tekedra Mawakana.

Waymo, which was valued at $110bn in February, is expanding at a rapid pace across the US. Its robotaxi service is live in 11 cities, taking passengers on more than 500,000 journeys every week, and it is preparing to launch in another 20 markets.
European cities are lagging behind the US and China in deploying robotaxis, and Chinese competition has pushed Germany’s once-vibrant auto industry into decline.

The German government is looking to regain the industry’s momentum by embracing technology and has introduced a series of measures in recent years to allow driverless vehicles to operate on its streets.

“Autonomous driving is the key to the mobility of the future,” said Christian Hirte, parliamentary state secretary in the Federal Ministry of Transport. “We aim to make Germany a global leader in autonomous driving innovation and manufacturing. We have already put in place the legal framework for this.”

Bavaria is home to BMW and Audi’s headquarters, as well as hundreds of automotive suppliers. Several US big tech companies, including Google, Apple and Amazon, also have significant engineering operations in Munich, the Bavarian state capital.
Alongside Waymo’s announcement, Bavaria’s chancellery pledged to “cut red tape and remove regulatory barriers” to real-world deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs).
Waymo said it would soon begin the mapping and training process that precedes its launches, as it works with city, state and federal authorities to win the necessary regulatory approvals.
Recommended
The Silicon Valley-based company is joining an increasingly crowded market for AV testing in Germany.

Uber and Israeli start-up Autobrains said in June they planned to launch in Munich, while Lyft-owned Freenow and Apollo Go, Chinese tech company Baidu’s AV unit, have also said they hope to offer rides in Germany soon.

Momenta, another Chinese AV operator that has struck partnerships with Uber and Grab, said last month it had received approval for autonomous testing across the country from Germany’s vehicle safety authority.
Automakers have also targeted German cities as a gateway to expanding AVs across Europe.

Last month, Volkswagen launched its pilot robotaxi service in Hamburg, allowing the city’s preregistered residents to book rides in its ID. Buzz electric campervans. Its robotaxi unit, MOIA, has 100 taxi vehicles in Germany, Norway and the US, and is aiming to have 100,000 vehicles on the road globally by 2033.

/content/af815e45-b132-4db4-96bc-428f8e0.title: Nvidia employee charged with smuggling advanced chips into China
articleContent: An Nvidia employee has been charged in Taiwan with smuggling advanced AI chips into China in the first known indictment of a worker at the US chipmaker over alleged illegal exports.
Taiwan’s Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office charged nine people, including employees of server maker Super Micro Computer, on Monday with illegally selling high-end AI servers to Chinese customers.
Prosecutors accused the defendants of colluding in pursuit of huge profits and “seriously damaging Taiwan’s international image”. Many of Nvidia’s chips and servers are made on the island.
They described a Taiwan-based senior manager at Nvidia surnamed Zhang as the “central figure” in a scheme involving 130 of the chipmaker’s flagship B300 servers.

The B300 is a popular server for training AI models and contains Nvidia’s advanced chips. The servers are subject to US export controls as Washington tries to constrain China’s ability to develop cutting-edge AI.
Washington’s restrictions have created a lucrative black market under which prices can double or triple.

Prosecutors said Zhang, two senior Super Micro salespeople, a Taiwanese distributor and other intermediaries colluded to circumvent customer checks by Nvidia and Super Micro, which is one of several companies that package Nvidia’s AI chips into servers.
They alleged that defendants falsely claimed the servers would be used in a data centre in Taiwan, even though its electricity supply and network bandwidth were insufficient to operate them.

Of the 130 servers, 74 were ultimately shipped to Chinese customers, according to prosecutors, either directly from Taiwan or routed through Indonesia or Japan. The remaining 56 were stopped by Taiwan’s customs officials.
Recommended
Zhang allegedly helped secure an allocation of servers and participated in an inspection of the data centre where they would purportedly be used.
Prosecutors said he deliberately concealed that the data-centre buyer lacked sufficient financial resources and that the funds used to purchase the servers actually came from a Chinese company.
They have requested the statutory maximum sentence of five years in prison for Zhang and three other defendants, while the other five were recommended for shorter terms.

Nvidia said: “Our employees have every incentive to work diligently with customers to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible.”

Super Micro said its “co-operation with Taiwanese authorities led to the arrests of the indicted individuals” and that it was “not a target of their investigation and has not been accused of any wrongdoing”.
Additional reporting by Michael Acton in San Francisco

/content/f4a1aa36-761b-4b5a-86a4-4be9abc.title: The little-known French company trying to unseat Palantir in Europe
articleContent: A little-known French software group is seeking to position itself as the European answer to Palantir as governments across the region try to cut their reliance on US tech companies.

ChapsVision, which won a French government contract in June to replace Palantir at the country’s domestic intelligence agency, is in talks with governments across the EU and competing for major German defence and police contracts.
Its pitch is that Europe’s sovereignty concerns, combined with growing unease over Palantir’s political ties and operating model, have created an opening for a European-owned data platform.
“We are not, and we do not wish to be, a black box . . . Our algorithms, our architecture, and our code are transparent. They are open,” ChapsVision group general manager Silvano Sansoni told the FT.

The French project also includes contracts to create the data infrastructure for all government ministries and about 50 public agencies, setting up a wide-ranging test case for whether a sovereign solution can be deployed at this scale.
Palantir, whose software is widely used by US defence and intelligence agencies, has faced growing scrutiny in parts of Europe as governments reassess their dependence on US technology companies.
Germany’s armed forces have excluded Palantir from contracts, while officials in Denmark and the Netherlands have also said they want to uncouple from the US-based software group.

Swiss authorities have declined to adopt its software, while in the UK a £330mn deal for the health service has faced significant scrutiny and London’s mayor vetoed a £50mn contract with the city’s Metropolitan Police.

Beyond the sovereignty argument, ChapsVision is also challenging Palantir’s business model. Sansoni said ChapsVision’s software did not require the long-term dependence on embedded engineers that has become a hallmark of Palantir’s approach.

“Our goal is to transfer the skills to the client and then move on to the next project. We, as a software publisher, don’t aim to stay with the client for 10 or 40 years and, so to speak, take over their business. This is somewhat different from Palantir’s approach.”
Paris-based ChapsVision, whose name derives from the first initials of founder Olivier Dellenbach’s children, first started out in 2019 developing tools for financial services.

It has since grown to about €200mn in annual revenues, with much of that growth coming from acquisitions. It has made nearly 30 acquisitions to date, buying in expertise in areas including translation AI, defence software and semantic search as it tries to become a European data champion.

While half of its business is from the public sector, it also works for large companies such as Pfizer, LVMH, L’Oréal, Airbus, Safran, ExxonMobil, Total and AstraZeneca. With backing from investors including Bpifrance, Tikehau, Jolt and Qalium, ChapsVision is considering a potential initial public offering by the end of the decade.

Europe’s drive for tech sovereignty has already helped the company win a German intelligence contract this year. It is also competing with Palantir for two major German contracts, covering North Rhine-Westphalia police and the Bundeswehr.

The rollout of ChapsVision’s software across France’s domestic intelligence agency will test whether the country can replace a critical US software platform with a domestic alternative after years of mixed success with state-backed digital projects.

Under French President Emmanuel Macron, France has sought to champion domestic technologies, though several state-backed digital projects have suffered from fragmented procurement, technical flaws or limited adoption.

“The move from Palantir to ChapsVision is first and foremost a political manoeuvre,” said Charles Thibout, an expert in digital transformations and technology at the Institute for International and Strategic Relations.

“The question we can ask ourselves is whether this is truly a strategic choice, informed by a clear awareness of the stakes and ChapsVision’s technological capabilities, or rather a public relations move to silence criticism about the government’s close ties with major American tech companies,” he added.
Recommended

The migration from Palantir to ChapsVision’s tools in French intelligence is expected to take up to two years while the government expands computing capacity, transfers intelligence data and trains officials.

“The product is ready, we have worked on it for four years . . . but it is the client who determines the timeline,” said Sansoni, adding that the company’s “goal” now was to secure other large-scale public projects on the back of this one.
But ChapsVision faces an uphill battle against its much bigger rival Palantir, which has a market cap of $418bn and reported annual revenues of $4.5bn in 2025.
Sansoni noted that “humility is important”, given ChapsVision is up against a company with “much larger investments”.
“But we have still managed to position ourselves on differentiating factors for customers. We have mainly looked for the areas where one would say Palantir is less effective.”

/content/c36d4e57-1ea2-47a5-8f6d-f390369.title: SEC subpoenas Wall Street banks over Situational Awareness
articleContent: The Securities and Exchange Commission has subpoenaed some of the largest Wall Street banks that helped fund trading bets at Situational Awareness before the hedge fund was nearly toppled in the recent tech sell-off.

The US financial markets regulator requested detailed information about Situational Awareness’s trades and its communication with the lenders that provided it with leverage, according to two people familiar with the probe.

The hedge fund was a client of Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Citigroup and Bank of America, according to regulatory filings. Lending to hedge funds has become an increasingly important and lucrative business line for Wall Street banks in recent years.

The AI-focused hedge fund run by 24-year-old OpenAI alumnus Leopold Aschenbrenner amassed more than $20bn in assets in less than two years and achieved astronomical gains, using borrowed money to amplify its concentrated bets on AI-linked stocks.

Situational Awareness ran into difficulty during the intense tech sell-off in July, becoming the biggest casualty of the market downswing. After facing steep losses, the San Francisco-based firm was forced to sell the majority of its stock holdings to Citadel in an emergency transaction pulled together in just 24 hours.

“It is to be expected that regulators would closely examine any funds that are high-profile, produce significant returns, or have particularly dramatic drawdowns,” Situational Awareness said in a statement. “We are a highly regulated business and will co-operate to the fullest extent with any regulatory request.”
Recommended
The fund has not been accused of wrongdoing. One person cautioned that the SEC probe was simply in the “information-gathering” stage.
Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan declined to comment. The SEC also declined to comment.

In the aftermath of the deal with Citadel, Aschenbrenner has said he took “full responsibility” for the events that led to the rapid losses. He said the fund would continue to operate and trade public equities but would no longer borrow from banks to fund his bets.

Citadel purchased the positions at a roughly 10 per cent discount, the FT has previously reported. Earlier this month, Ken Griffin’s hedge fund told investors the firm had sold more than 80 per cent of the portfolio via almost 100 block trades worth more than $4bn.
The New York Times first reported the subpoenas.
Additional reporting by Kaye Wiggins

/content/5ee49718-c258-4f01-aa32-7e5b76a.title: Anthropic’s best AI model struggles to attract users as cheaper tools thrive
articleContent: Anthropic’s US customers are using cheaper alternatives to its most powerful AI tool, raising questions about the group’s high-spending business model ahead of what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time.

Spending on Fable 5, Anthropic’s largest and priciest model, has plateaued at only about 11 per cent of overall outlay on the company’s tools, more than two months after its release, according to spending data from 70,000 companies collected by payments group Ramp.

This breaks a pattern of corporate users defaulting to the most powerful models. Analysts and investors in Anthropic said the change was primarily driven by Fable’s high price and the fact that older models are capable of handling the bulk of business demands.

If sustained, the shift could radically alter the business model of frontier labs, which have until now funnelled the bulk of their multibillion-dollar development spending towards training larger, more sophisticated models.

“Most people don’t need to operate at the frontier,” said Miles Clements, a partner at Accel, which has invested close to $1bn in Anthropic. The period in which customers tended to choose only the frontier models “was not a durable era”, he added.

Breakthroughs in intelligence remain essential to fulfil the companies’ loftiest promises, such as curing disease, and to attract the best researchers. But they will increasingly be showcases, said Clements.
Fable 5’s launch in early June was disrupted by Donald Trump’s administration, which forced Anthropic to withdraw the model, citing national security concerns.

Concerns about further limits on access to Fable have receded since the White House greenlit its relaunch on July 1. Political uncertainty has become a secondary factor, compared with price and performance, in driving clients’ model choice, according to analysts and investors.

The lower demand for Fable, which has had a slower rate of take-up than previous cutting-edge releases, adds to the uncertainty for Anthropic ahead of its IPO, which investors anticipate will value the group at $2tn or more and could come as soon as next month.

Anthropic’s revenue in July undershot the most bullish expectations from investors, who projected annualised sales would cross $80bn. Anthropic told shareholders last week that its revenue last month hit $65bn on an annualised basis, up from $47bn in May.
Still, the start-up led by chief executive Dario Amodei continues to grow at a blistering pace, with revenue increasing nearly sevenfold since the start of the year.

Anthropic recorded its first adjusted operating profit in the second quarter of the year and has guided investors that it is likely to be profitable again in the third quarter, according to people with knowledge of the matter. It also told investors that it had 6,000 customers that spend $100,000 annually or more.
The company declined to comment.
Businesses are trying to contain spending on AI by using models more efficiently rather than always going with the most sophisticated option.

The availability of cheap, open-weight models from China and elsewhere has provided customers with more alternatives to the leading US labs, while there are also signs that Sam Altman’s OpenAI is gaining ground after slipping back for much of 2026.

The ChatGPT maker’s annualised revenue has jumped 35 per cent in the quarter to date and is now more than $40bn, with the launch of GPT 5.6 in July jolting the company’s performance after a sluggish start to the year, said people with knowledge of the matter.
Recommended

GPT 5.6 is priced significantly lower than Fable 5. Anthropic’s Opus 5, a smaller but nevertheless potent model that comes at a lower price, has surpassed Fable in terms of business spending since its launch in late July, according to Ramp.
Anthropic’s revenue growth took a hit in June, largely because of the US government’s decision to limit the rollout of Fable, but has since rebounded.
Data retention rules imposed by the Trump administration have also hampered Fable’s adoption, according to Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp.

Kharazian said predicting the company’s trajectory even months ahead is a virtually impossible task. “If you impute previous trends you expect Anthropic to own the market. But because [OpenAI’s newest model] was so good and Fable underperformed, it’s been the reverse,” he added.
